teile.einleitung: A **dry stone wall** is built entirely without mortar. The stones hold together only through clever layering. In its cracks and gaps, many plants and animals live.
wichtigste: A dry stone wall holds without mortar, just through clever layering.
On steep slopes it was used to build terraces for vines and fields.
A retaining wall is built leaning slightly back towards the slope.
Water can drain away through the joints, so it lasts a long time.
Lizards, snakes and wild bees like to live in dry stone walls.
In 2018 the art of dry stone walling was added to the UNESCO list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

abschnitte.text: In a dry stone wall, stones are laid on top of each other so that they support one another. **Only their clever layering** holds them together. Large stones go at the bottom, and the joints are staggered, as in a puzzle. Gaps are filled with small stones. A good **retaining wall** on a slope **leans slightly back towards the slope**, so the earth does not push it over.

In the past, many dry stone walls were built on steep slopes **to create terraces for vines and fields**. This produced flat land that could be worked. In Switzerland the vineyard terraces of **Lavaux** on Lake Geneva are famous and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. There are also many such walls in the Valais and in Ticino. Because **water can drain away through the joints**, no pressure builds up behind the wall, and it often lasts a very long time.

The stones of a dry stone wall **store the sun’s heat**. That is why **lizards and snakes** love these walls, as they need warmth to be active. The **wall lizard** even carries the wall in its name. In the joints of sunny walls, **wild bees** build their nests. Snails, spiders and beetles also find hiding places.

In the cracks grow plants that manage with little soil and water. The **biting stonecrop** has thick leaves in which it **stores water**. Ferns such as wall-rue and small flowers also settle there. That way an old dry stone wall becomes a colourful habitat. In **2018**, the art of dry stone walling was added to the UNESCO list of **Intangible Cultural Heritage**, jointly by several countries, including Switzerland.

gewusst: Some dry stone walls have stood for many centuries.
A dry stone wall can be repaired by resetting individual stones, without tearing down the whole wall.

teile.einleitung: **Clay minerals** are tiny mineral platelets found in almost every soil. They make clay sticky and easy to shape. They are important for plants because they hold on to water and nutrients.
wichtigste: Clay minerals belong to the phyllosilicates.
They form mainly through chemical weathering of feldspars and micas.
Kaolinite is a two-layer mineral and hardly swells at all.
Montmorillonite swells strongly and is the main component of bentonite.
In illite, potassium is firmly built in between the layers.
Their negatively charged surface binds nutrients such as calcium and potassium.
In Switzerland, Opalinus Clay is planned for a deep repository.

abschnitte.text: Clay minerals belong to the group of **phyllosilicates**. They consist of thin layers that lie on top of each other like the pages of a book. The building blocks are mainly silicon, aluminium and oxygen. The individual particles are **tiny, thin platelets**, much smaller than a grain of sand. That is why clay minerals have a huge **specific surface area**: even one gram of clay has a very large surface.

Clay minerals form mainly through **chemical weathering**. Water and acids slowly attack rocks such as granite. In the process, **feldspars** and **micas** are changed. Over a long time, new, very fine minerals are made from them. Depending on the climate and the rock, different clay minerals form.

**Kaolinite** is a **two-layer mineral** and hardly swells. It is used, for example, to make porcelain. **Montmorillonite** can take up a lot of water between its layers and **swells strongly**. It is the main component of **bentonite**, a clay used for sealing. In **illite**, **potassium** sits firmly between the layers and stops it from swelling.

The surfaces of clay minerals are **negatively charged**. That is why they hold on to positively charged particles, called **cations**. These include important nutrients such as calcium, magnesium and potassium. Plant roots can later exchange them again and take them up. How many cations a soil can bind in this way is called the **cation exchange capacity**. Soils rich in clay are therefore often fertile.

**Opalinus Clay** is a clay-rich rock that formed about 175 million years ago. It is very dense and lets hardly any water through. That is why in Switzerland it is planned as the **host rock** for a geological **deep repository** for radioactive waste. In 2022, Nagra proposed the Nördlich Lägern area for this. In the Mont Terri rock laboratory in the Jura, Opalinus Clay has been studied for years.

gewusst: Swelling clay can seal fine cracks by itself again when it takes up water.
The word kaolinite comes from the Chinese place Gaoling, where porcelain clay used to be mined.

teile.einleitung: The **forget-me-not** is a small flower with sky-blue blossoms. It blooms in spring in many gardens. Its name recalls friendship and remembrance.
wichtigste: The flowers of the forget-me-not are mostly light blue.
In the middle sits a small yellow ring.
Each flower has five petals and is only a few millimetres across.
The buds are often pink and turn blue as they open.
The forget-me-not blooms in spring.
The water forget-me-not grows by water.

abschnitte.text: The flowers of the forget-me-not are mostly **light blue**. They are very small, only a few millimetres across. But many flowers stand together in clusters. Each flower has **five petals**. They are arranged around a small **yellow centre**.
The yellow ring in the middle is not just pretty. It shows insects the way to the **nectar**. Bees, flies and butterflies visit the flowers. In doing so they carry pollen from flower to flower.

The buds of the forget-me-not are often **pink**. As they open, the flowers turn blue. On one plant you can therefore sometimes see both colours at once. In the garden the forget-me-not blooms in **spring**, often together with tulips. After that it fades.
There are different kinds of forget-me-not. The **water forget-me-not** loves wet soil. You find it by streams, ponds and in marshes. Other kinds grow in meadows, in the woods or in the garden.

The name says: forget me not, so **think of me**. That is why the flower is given as a sign of **remembrance** and friendship. In other languages, too, the flower has a similar name, for example “Vergissmeinnicht” in German.

gewusst: In German, the forget-me-not is called “Vergissmeinnicht”, which means exactly the same.
On one flower cluster you can see pink buds and blue flowers at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Trees have to transport water from the roots up to the crown. In conifers, this is done mainly by **tracheids**. These long, dead cells carry water and at the same time make the wood strong.
wichtigste: Tracheids are long, dead cells with pointed ends and pits.
Softwood consists mainly of tracheids.
They carry water and strengthen the wood.
Their walls are made woody by lignin and can withstand pressure.
Vessels, by contrast, have perforated cross walls.
In the bordered pit sits a thickened middle part, the torus.

abschnitte.text: A **tracheid** is a **long, dead cell** with **pointed ends**. When it is fully built, its inside dies off, and only the firm wall is left. This wall is made woody with **lignin** and so can **withstand pressure**. Through small spots in the wall, the **pits**, water flows from one tracheid into the next. In softwood, tracheids make up most of the wood.

Broadleaved trees also have **vessels**. They consist of many cells whose **cross walls are perforated**. This produces long, wide tubes through which water flows quickly. Tracheids, by contrast, are single, narrow cells. The water has to pass from cell to cell through the pits, which is slower, but safer.

In drought or frost, **gas bubbles** can form in the water pipes. An **embolism** like this interrupts the water transport. In a wide vessel, one bubble can block a long tube. In tracheids, **the bubble stays limited to one small cell**. In the **bordered pits** sits a thickened middle part, the **torus**. It can close the pit like a valve so that the air does not spread.

In softwood, tracheids perform **two jobs at once**: **carrying water and providing strength**. In spring the tree forms wide, thin-walled tracheids, the light **earlywood**. In summer, **thick-walled** tracheids with a **narrow lumen** form, the darker **latewood**. Through this alternation, clear **annual rings** can be seen in the wood. From them you can tell the age of a tree.

gewusst: Even the earliest land plants over 400 million years ago had tracheids.
A tracheid in spruce wood is only a few millimetres long, but much longer than it is wide.

teile.einleitung: Urban gardening means gardening in the city. People grow vegetables, herbs and flowers on roofs, in back yards or on wasteland, often together with others.
wichtigste: Urban gardening means gardening in the city.
Growing is often done communally on wasteland, roofs or in back yards.
On sealed surfaces, people garden in crates, sacks and raised beds.
In Switzerland many city dwellers rent an allotment garden.
The German city of Andernach became known as the “Edible City”.
Soils beside busy roads can contain heavy metals such as lead.

abschnitte.titel: Green in the middle of the city
abschnitte.text: In **urban gardening**, people garden in the city. They grow tomatoes, lettuce, herbs or flowers on unused areas. Often this is done **communally**: neighbours share a garden, swap knowledge and harvest together. That creates green places where people meet. At the same time bees and butterflies find food.

In the city the ground is often **sealed**, that is, covered with concrete or asphalt. That is why, on roofs or car parks, people often garden in **crates, sacks and raised beds**. They bring the soil there and can be moved if needed. A well-known example is the **Prinzessinnengarten** in Berlin-Kreuzberg. It was created on wasteland at Moritzplatz, where gardening was done in mobile crates.

In Switzerland there have long been **allotment gardens**. Many cities rent out plots on shared sites, and in Germany they are called “Schrebergärten” or “Kleingärten”. The German city of **Andernach** on the Rhine took a different path. As the **“Edible City”**, it plants vegetables, herbs and fruit in public spaces, and the population may harvest them.

In **guerrilla gardening**, public spaces such as wasteland or the soil around trees are planted without permission. Often **seed bombs** made of soil, clay and seeds are used. Quite different is **vertical farming**: plants grow in buildings on many levels one above another, often under artificial light. That way a lot can be produced on a small footprint.

Not every city soil is clean. Traffic and old contaminated sites can burden the soil with **heavy metals** such as **lead**. Vegetables right beside busy roads can take up these substances. That is why it is worth having the soil tested before growing, or gardening in crates with fresh soil.

gewusst: Even a balcony can be a small city garden, for example with herbs in pots.
Community gardens are often also places where children learn where vegetables come from.

teile.einleitung: The martagon lily, called “Türkenbund” (Turk’s turban) in German, is a wild lily that grows in light woods and on mountain meadows. Its nodding, pink to purple flowers are reminiscent of a turban.
wichtigste: The martagon lily is a lily and usually grows 30 to 150 centimetres tall.
Its flowers hang downwards, and the petals are rolled far back.
It flowers pink to purplish red with dark spots.
Hawk-moths such as the hummingbird hawk-moth pollinate it, especially in the evening.
One stem can bear up to 20 flowers.
Because of its golden-yellow bulb it used to be called golden root.

abschnitte.text: The German name comes from the special shape of the flower. The petals are strongly **rolled back**. That makes the flower look like a **turban**, a wound headscarf. The stamens then hang freely downwards. The flowers **nod downwards** and hang on long stalks.

The martagon lily mostly flowers **pink to purplish red**. Dark spots sit on the petals. The plant usually grows **30 to 150 centimetres** tall. One stem often bears several flowers, and in sunny places there can be **up to 20**. The leaves stand in tiers around the stem. It flowers in summer.

The martagon lily smells strongest in the **evening** and at night. With this it attracts **hawk-moths**, a group of moths with a very long proboscis. A well-known example is the **hummingbird hawk-moth**. It hovers in the air in front of the flower and collects the nectar. In doing so it carries pollen from flower to flower.

The martagon lily likes cool, **half-shaded places** in light woods. In the mountains it also grows on **mountain meadows** and in tall herb communities. In Switzerland you can find it mainly in the Alps and the Jura. Because it has become rare, it should not be picked or dug up.

Under the ground, the martagon lily has a **golden-yellow bulb**. That is why it used to be called **golden root**. Some people even believed that you could make gold with it. Of course that never worked.

gewusst: The martagon lily belongs to the same genus as the large garden lilies.
A hummingbird hawk-moth can hover in the air in front of a flower like a hummingbird.

teile.einleitung: You can recognise the **weeping willow** at once by its long branches that hang down to the ground. It often stands by ponds, lakes and in parks. It originally comes from China.
wichtigste: The branches of the weeping willow hang down to the ground.
It belongs to the willows.
It originally comes from China.
Its leaves are long and narrow.
It is often planted at the edge of ponds and lakes.
It grows quickly, and a twig in damp soil often forms roots.

abschnitte.text: The weeping willow is a medium-sized tree with a broad crown. Its thin, flexible branches **hang down to the ground** and move even in a light wind. The **leaves** are **long and narrow**, green on top and paler underneath. In spring it comes into leaf early and glows light green. It belongs **to the willows**, like the goat willow or the white willow.

The weeping willow originally comes **from China**. Along trade routes it came west and later to Europe. Its scientific name is **Salix babylonica**, because it used to be wrongly believed to come from Babylon. Many weeping willows in our parks are crosses with other kinds of willow. They put up with winter better here.

Willows love damp soil. That is why weeping willows are often planted **at the edge of ponds and lakes**, where their branches reach down into the water. The weeping willow **grows quickly**. If you stick a willow twig into damp soil, **it often forms roots** and becomes a new tree. Willow wood is rather soft and light.

The hanging branches remind many people of mourning and **farewell**. That is how the tree got its name. In the past, weeping willows were often planted **in cemeteries**. Today you see them mainly in parks and gardens, for example on Swiss lakeside promenades. The weeping willow also often appears in poems and pictures.

gewusst: The bark of willows contains salicin, a substance from which remedies for pain and fever were once obtained.
Willow twigs are so flexible that baskets can be woven from them.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes a whole new plant can grow from a single leaf. This is due to an astonishing ability of many plant cells: **totipotency**. Nurseries and laboratories use it to propagate plants.
wichtigste: A totipotent plant cell can give rise to a whole plant.
Specialised cells can dedifferentiate and divide again.
In tissue cultures, a disorganised mass of cells forms, the callus.
Gottlieb Haberlandt predicted in 1902 that this is possible.
Frederick C. Steward showed it in the 1950s with carrot cells.
A lot of cytokinin in relation to auxin encourages the formation of shoots.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Latin: “totus” means whole, “potentia” means ability. A **totipotent** cell can therefore form a **whole plant** with roots, stem and leaves. In plants, many fully grown cells keep this ability. Cells that can form many, but not all, cell types are called **pluripotent**.

In a plant, most cells have a fixed job, for example as a leaf cell or a root cell. They are said to be **differentiated**. Under certain conditions they can give up this specialisation and **become able to divide again**. This is called **dedifferentiation**. That is why a whole new plant can grow from a **leaf cutting** of an **African violet**.

In **tissue culture**, small pieces of plant are placed on a nutrient medium with sugar, salts and plant hormones. There a disorganised mass of cells grows first, the **callus**. With the hormones **cytokinin** and **auxin**, you control what becomes of it. A high ratio of cytokinin to auxin encourages the formation of **shoots**, while a lot of auxin tends to encourage roots. That way, for example, orchids or virus-free potatoes can be propagated in large numbers.

The Austrian botanist **Gottlieb Haberlandt** predicted as early as **1902** that isolated plant cells in culture could develop into whole plants. At that time, however, he did not manage to do it himself. In the **1950s**, the researcher **Frederick C. Steward** showed with cells from the **carrot** that it really works. Complete carrot plants grew from single cells.

gewusst: Plants propagated in this way from parts of a single mother plant are clones, that is, almost identical in their genes.
Haberlandt is regarded as the father of plant tissue culture.

teile.einleitung: In **grafting**, gardeners put a piece of a good variety onto another plant with roots. The two parts grow together. This is how fruit trees, roses and vines in particular are propagated.
wichtigste: The part put on is called the scion, the plant with roots the rootstock.
The cambium of both parts must touch so that they grow together.
In budding, a single bud is put into a T-shaped cut in the bark.
In whip grafting, parts of equal thickness are cut at a slant and joined.
The rootstock M9 gives small apple trees that bear fruit early.
Because of phylloxera, European vines are grafted onto American rootstocks.

abschnitte.text: The **scion** comes from the desired variety, for example a particular apple. The **rootstock** supplies the roots. It influences how strongly the tree grows and how robust it is. For the two parts to grow together, their **cambium** must touch. This is a thin, dividing layer of tissue under the bark.

In **budding**, only a single bud is put into a T-shaped cut in the bark. In German the name comes from the Latin oculus for eye, because the bud is also called an eye. In **whip grafting**, you cut rootstock and scion of equal thickness with slanting cuts of equal length. Then you lay them exactly on top of each other and bind them tightly.

Apple trees are mostly **heterozygous** and are pollinated by other trees. A little tree from a pip therefore differs clearly from the parent variety. A variety such as “Gala” would not be kept that way. That is why varieties are grafted. The rootstock **M9** comes from East Malling in England. It slows growth, so small trees arise that bear fruit early.

In the late 19th century, **phylloxera** was brought into Europe. It destroyed the roots of European vines. American vine roots are largely resistant. Since then, European varieties have been grafted onto **American rootstocks**. This also applies to many vineyards in Switzerland.
The graft union of a fruit tree is placed above the ground. If it lies in the soil, the scion can form roots of its own. Then the influence of the rootstock is lost, for example the weak growth.

gewusst: Several apple varieties can be grafted onto a single tree.
Almost all vines in Europe today stand on American roots.

teile.einleitung: The tundra is a treeless, cold landscape in the far north. The winter is long and dark, the summer short, and the ground stays frozen at depth all year round.
wichtigste: In the tundra it is too cold and the summer too short for trees.
Mosses, lichens, grasses and dwarf shrubs grow there.
Under the surface lies permanently frozen ground, the permafrost.
Reindeer move through the tundra in large herds, in North America they are called caribou.
The Arctic fox has a white coat in winter.
In summer in the far north, the sun does not set for days on end.

abschnitte.text: The tundra lies north of the great coniferous forests, the **taiga**. There it is cold for a very long time, and the summer lasts only a few weeks. Trees have too little time to grow. In between lies the **forest tundra**, where only single, low and crooked trees stand. Further north the open tundra begins.

In the tundra only low plants grow that can cope with cold and a short growing season. Typical are **mosses, lichens, grasses and dwarf shrubs**. Dwarf willows and dwarf birches hardly grow knee-high. Flat on the ground, they are protected from the icy wind. In the short summer the tundra often blooms in many colours.

Under the tundra lies the **permafrost**, ground that stays permanently frozen. In summer only the top layer thaws, the **active layer**. The water cannot drain down into the depths. That is why the ground is often wet despite little precipitation, and there are many **marshes and pools**. On a slope, the wet layer slowly slides downhill, which is called **solifluction**.

The best-known animals are the **reindeer**, which migrate in large herds. In North America they are called **caribou**. The **Arctic fox** has a white coat in winter and is well camouflaged in the snow. Other residents are lemmings, mountain hares and musk oxen. In summer many **migratory birds** come here to breed.

In summer in the far north, the sun does not set for days on end. This is called the **midnight sun**. In winter it is the other way round: then it stays dark for weeks, which is the **polar night**. In the Alps, too, above the tree line there is a similar landscape, called **alpine tundra**.

gewusst: If the permafrost thaws because of warming, houses and roads can sink.
Well-preserved mammoth remains have already been found in the frozen ground of the tundra.

teile.einleitung: Tulips are popular spring flowers with large, bright blooms. They grow from a bulb and originally come from Asia.
wichtigste: Tulip bulbs are planted in autumn and flower in spring.
Wild tulips come from the mountains of Central Asia.
A simple tulip has six petals in two circles.
The Netherlands is famous for its huge tulip fields.
Around 1637, a rare tulip bulb in Holland cost as much as a house.
In the Upper Valais grows the rare Grengiols tulip.

abschnitte.text: The tulip grows from a **bulb**. In it the plant stores nutrients for the next year. The bulbs are put into the ground in **autumn**. They need the **cold of winter** to flower in spring. After flowering, the plant draws its strength back into the bulb.

A simple tulip has **six petals**. They stand in two circles of three. Tulips come in very many colours: red, yellow, white, pink, purple and almost black. A **true, pure blue** has still not been bred. Cut tulips **keep growing in the vase**, and their stems get a few centimetres longer.

Wild tulips originally grow in **Asia**, for example in the mountains of Central Asia. In the Ottoman Empire, in what is now Turkey, they were very popular. From there they came to Europe in the 16th century. The name “tulip” comes from an old word for **turban**, because the flower is reminiscent of this headwear.

In Holland in the 17th century, tulips became a real craze. Rare varieties with flame-patterned flowers were in hot demand. Around **1637**, people paid as much for a single especially rare bulb as for a house. Then prices suddenly collapsed. This period is called **tulip mania**. To this day the **Netherlands** is famous for its colourful tulip fields and sells tulips all over the world.
In Switzerland too there is a very special tulip. The **Grengiols tulip** grows only near Grengiols in the **Upper Valais**. It is very rare. That is why it is protected and must not be picked.

gewusst: The flame patterns of the expensive tulips of tulip mania were caused by a plant virus.
Tulips often turn their flowers towards the light and close them again in the evening.

teile.einleitung: A trophic mismatch arises when an animal species needs its food most urgently at exactly the time when it is no longer most plentiful. Climate change can make such shifts in timing stronger.
wichtigste: Mismatch means roughly “not fitting together”.
What is meant is a decoupling in time between the need for food and the supply of food.
The idea comes from the British fisheries biologist David Cushing.
A textbook example is the pied flycatcher in the Netherlands.
Many migratory birds go by day length, plants and insects rather by temperature.
Reindeer in Greenland and wild bees can also be affected.

abschnitte.text: Many animals raise their young when there is the most food. But if predators and prey react differently to changes, the **peak of the food supply** no longer coincides with the time of greatest need. Then, for example, food is missing for the young birds. This decoupling in time is called a **trophic mismatch**.

The **match-mismatch hypothesis** was originally formulated by the British fisheries biologist **David Cushing**. He wanted to explain why some year classes of fish are strong and others weak. What matters, he suggested, is whether the larvae hatch at the time of the **plankton bloom**. Then they find enough food.

A well-studied example is the chain **oak, winter moth caterpillar, great tit**. The budburst of the oak determines when the caterpillars hatch. The tits need many caterpillars at exactly that time for their nestlings. With warming, these dates shift by different amounts. In the Netherlands the **pied flycatcher** became the textbook example: it returns from West Africa when the caterpillar peak may already be over.

abschnitte.titel: Why migratory birds are especially affected
abschnitte.text: Many migratory birds set off according to **day length**, and this does not change with the climate. Plants and insects, on the other hand, react more strongly to **temperature**. Long-distance migrants in winter quarters south of the Sahara cannot sense how early spring begins in Europe. Short-distance migrants can adjust their return more easily.

In West Greenland, plant growth began earlier because of warming. But the calves of the **reindeer** were not born correspondingly earlier and missed the most nutritious food. A mismatch also threatens between **early flowering plants and wild bees**: if plants flower too early, the pollinators are missing, and the bees find less food later.

gewusst: The numbers of the pied flycatcher fell most where the caterpillar peak came especially early.
Some bird species have already moved their breeding season forward somewhat in recent decades.

teile.einleitung: The growing season is the time of year in which plants can grow, flower and form seeds. In the high mountains it is much shorter than on the Central Plateau, and plants have developed special tricks.
wichtigste: The growing season is the time with enough warmth and light for plant growth.
In the alpine zone it lasts only about two to three months.
For every 100 metres of climb, it gets about 0.5 to 0.7 degrees cooler on average.
Almost all high-mountain plants are perennial.
Many form their flower buds as early as the previous year.
First frosts and snowfalls often end the growing season as early as September.

abschnitte.text: Plants need **warmth and light** to grow. The time of year in which both are enough is called the **growing season**. On the Central Plateau it lasts many months. In the high mountains, on the other hand, snow lies for a long time, and frost returns early. In the **alpine zone**, therefore, only about **two to three months** are left for growing, flowering and forming seeds.

With increasing height the air becomes cooler. On average the temperature falls by about **0.5 to 0.7 degrees per 100 metres**. In addition the snow melts later up high. That is why the warm season begins much later at altitude. The **dandelion** on an alpine pasture therefore flowers only weeks after the dandelion in the valley. And as early as **September**, first frosts and snowfalls can end the growing season.

Alpine plants have to be quick. Many form their **flower buds as early as the previous year**, in the late summer before. In spring they only have to open them. In addition, many plants store **sugar and starch** in roots or underground shoots in late summer. With this they can start growing straight after the snow melts.

An annual plant has to germinate, grow, flower and form seeds in a single summer. In the short mountain summer this rarely succeeds. That is why almost all high-mountain plants are **perennial** and live for many years. Because it is uncertain whether enough seeds will ripen, many also reproduce by **runners, bulbils or offshoots**.

After the short summer, the plants rest until the next year. The snow acts like a **warm blanket**. Under it, it is less cold than in the icy air above. With climate change, the growing season is getting longer in many areas, because the snow melts earlier.

gewusst: The alpine snowbell can even push its flower through a thin layer of snow.
Some Alpine plants live for many decades, even though they are only a few centimetres tall.

teile.einleitung: A trophic cascade arises when a predator has an effect across several steps of the food chain. If it eats plant eaters, the plants can increase as a result.
wichtigste: In a trophic cascade, a predator acts indirectly all the way down to the plants.
A well-known example: the return of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 and 1996.
The main prey of these wolves is elk.
When predators control the system, it is called top-down control.
Even the fear of predators changes the behaviour of prey animals.
In biomanipulation, predatory fish are introduced to make lakes clearer.

abschnitte.text: You can imagine a food chain like a staircase. If something changes at the top, you feel it further down. An example from the meadow: spiders eat grasshoppers, grasshoppers eat grass. If the **spiders** increase, there are fewer or more cautious grasshoppers, and the **grass** increases. This domino effect is called a **trophic cascade**.

In Yellowstone National Park in the USA, wolves were missing for about 70 years. In **1995 and 1996**, wolves from Canada were reintroduced there. Their main prey is **elk**, a large kind of deer. Fewer elk and more cautious behaviour can take pressure off the plants along the banks. How strong this effect is, is still debated among experts today.

Predators do not only act by eating prey. Even their presence changes where and for how long prey animals feed. This is called the **landscape of fear**. Dangerous places are avoided, and plants can grow better there. In Swiss mountain forests, it is expected that wolves keep red deer and roe deer on the move and that in some places fewer **young trees are browsed** as a result.

Ecologists distinguish two kinds of control. In **top-down control**, predators at the top determine the size of the lower levels. In **bottom-up control**, nutrients and plants limit the whole system. The **green world hypothesis** of 1960 says: the world is green because predators keep the plant eaters in check.

Knowledge about cascades is also put to use. In **biomanipulation**, predatory fish such as **pike** are introduced into lakes. They eat small fish that feed on zooplankton. As a result the **zooplankton** grows, which in turn eats algae. The water can become clearer in this way.

gewusst: A famous example from the sea: sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp. Where sea otters live, dense kelp forests often grow.
The green world hypothesis comes from the researchers Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin.

teile.einleitung: Even hard rocks do not stay the same for ever. Water, ice, warmth and living things slowly break up the rock. This process is called **weathering**.
wichtigste: In frost shattering, water freezes in cracks and bursts the rock apart.
Water expands by about 9 per cent when it freezes.
In the Alps, frost weathering is especially important.
Water with carbonic acid slowly dissolves limestone.
In biological weathering, roots, for example, burst rocks apart.
At the foot of rock faces, stones collect into scree slopes.
From weathered rock, sand, silt and clay arise for the soil.

abschnitte.text: Water penetrates fine cracks in the rock. When it freezes, ice needs more room than water. The volume increases by about **9 per cent**. The ice pushes the crack apart and bursts the rock. This is called **frost shattering**. In the high mountains of the **Alps** it freezes and thaws very often, so frost weathering is especially important there.

In deserts it is very hot by day and cold at night. Rock expands in heat and contracts in cold. These stresses make the surface flake off over time. This is **temperature weathering**. Together with frost shattering it belongs to **physical weathering**, in which rock is only broken up.

Rainwater takes up **carbon dioxide** from the air and so becomes slightly acidic. This water with **carbonic acid** slowly dissolves limestone. In this way, for example, **caves** and karren arise, which are grooves in limestone mountains. In Switzerland such forms are found, for example, in the Jura and in the limestone Alps.
Plants and animals also weather rock. Growing **roots** push cracks open and so burst rocks apart. **Lichens** attack the rock surface. This is called **biological weathering**.

Through weathering, stones break out of rock faces and fall down. At the foot of the wall they collect into a **scree slope**. Over time the rock breaks down into ever smaller grains: **sand**, **silt** and **clay**. Together with **humus** from dead plants, they form the soil.

gewusst: Without weathering there would be no soil in which plants could grow.
Large stalactite caves were formed by water that dissolved limestone over a very long time.

teile.einleitung: Dutch elm disease is a tree disease that has killed millions of elms in Europe. It is caused by a fungus that small beetles carry from tree to tree.
wichtigste: Dutch elm disease is caused by sac fungi of the genus Ophiostoma.
Elm bark beetles transmit the fungal spores from sick to healthy trees.
The fungus blocks the water pipes in the wood, and the leaves wilt.
The first big wave began around 1920 in Europe.
In the 1960s a more aggressive form came from North America.
In Switzerland the wych elm is the most common kind of elm.

abschnitte.text: Dutch elm disease is caused by **sac fungi** of the genus **Ophiostoma**. They penetrate the wood of the elms. The tree tries to stop the fungus and seals off its **conducting channels**. As a result, no more water reaches the crown. The leaves wilt and turn brown. Many infected trees die within a short time.

The fungus is carried from tree to tree by **elm bark beetles**. They breed under the bark of sick or dead elms. The young beetles take **fungal spores** with them. When they later feed on healthy elms, they infect them. That is how the disease spreads quickly.

People often speak of **Dutch elm disease**, although it did not come from the Netherlands. In the 1920s, however, Dutch researchers found out that a fungus causes the disease. They were **Bea Schwarz** and **Christine Buisman**. That is where the name comes from.

Shortly after the First World War, the first sick elms were noticed in France and the Netherlands. Around **1920** the first big wave began in Europe. In the **1960s**, a new, much **more aggressive fungus** reached Great Britain with timber deliveries from Canada. This second wave killed millions of elms in Europe. In many landscapes, large, old elms almost completely disappeared.

Three kinds of elm are native to Switzerland. The most widespread is the **wych elm**, which grows in damp, cool ravine and slope forests. Less common are the **field elm** and the **European white elm**. You can recognise elms by their fruits: the seed sits in the middle of a **round, flat wing**. That way the wind carries the fruits far away.

gewusst: Young elms often only become sick when they are bigger. That is why there are still many young elms, but only a few old ones.
Researchers are breeding elms that are less susceptible to the disease.

teile.einleitung: Many plants carry fine hairs on their leaves and stems. In scientific language these little hairs are called **trichomes**. In the mountains especially, they are an important protection against cold, sun and drought.
wichtigste: Trichomes are fine hairs on leaves and stems.
The edelweiss is covered with dense, white woolly hairs.
Densely hairy parts look silvery, because air between the hairs reflects the light.
The hairs keep a calm, damp layer of air at the leaf and so protect against drying out.
Light-coloured hairs block some of the UV rays.
On cold nights they hold in heat like a jumper.

abschnitte.text: **Trichomes** are outgrowths of the outermost layer of cells of a plant, the epidermis. They can be single-celled or multicellular, short or long, simple or branched. Some are **glandular hairs** that produce scented substances, as in thyme. Others are **stinging hairs**, as in the stinging nettle. Many plants, however, simply carry dense, soft **woolly hairs**.

Densely hairy plant parts often look **silvery or white**. This is not due to a pigment. **Air between the hairs** reflects the light, much as with snow. The best-known example is the **edelweiss**. The white, hairy **star-shaped rays** around its flower heads are not petals, but **bracts**. They act like a shield and **attract insects**.

In the Alps the sun is strong, especially the **UV radiation**. Light-coloured hairs **block some of the UV rays**, much like a sun hat. In addition, wind often blows and dries out leaves. A dense covering of hair **keeps a calm, damp layer of air** right at the leaf. That way less water evaporates.

On mountain nights it often gets very cold, even in summer. The hairs hold on to air and **so hold in heat like a jumper**. The **pasqueflower** flowers as early as spring, when it is still cold. It wears a furry coat of hairs and is therefore also called the **fur anemone**. Many other Alpine plants are also noticeably hairy.

gewusst: The edelweiss is a symbolic plant of the Alps and a well-known emblem in Switzerland.
The hairs of the stinging nettle break off when touched like tiny glass needles and squirt their burning sap into the skin.

teile.einleitung: A lake is divided into different zones from the shore to the middle. Depending on the depth of the water and the light, quite different plants grow there, and this is called lake zonation.
wichtigste: From the land to the deep water follow carr woodland, reed bed, floating-leaf zone and submerged zone.
The shore zone in which light reaches the bottom is called the littoral.
The dark, deep lake bed is called the profundal.
The open water in the middle of the lake is called the open-water zone or pelagial.
Water plants grow only as deep as enough light gets to.
In summer, warm water, the epilimnion, lies above cold deep water.

abschnitte.text: At the edge of many lakes grows a wet **carr woodland**. It is often shaped by the **black alder**, which tolerates ground that is sometimes flooded. Then follows the **reed bed** with reed and bulrush, which stand in shallow water. Further out begins the **floating-leaf zone**. There the leaves of water lilies and yellow water lilies lie on the surface of the water.

In the **submerged zone**, plants live completely under water, for example **pondweeds** and waterweed. In clear lakes, a zone with **stoneworts** often follows even further down. They manage with very little light and form dense lawns. Their name in German comes from the whorled branches, which are reminiscent of a candelabra.

Plants need light for **photosynthesis**. With increasing depth, the light is swallowed up by the water. At some point it is no longer enough, and plants stop growing. That is why the shore zone in which light reaches the bottom is called the **littoral**. All the water plants grow here. The clearer a lake is, the deeper this zone reaches.

The deep lake bed, where hardly any light gets, is called the **profundal**. No plants grow there, but bacteria and worms break down dead matter that sinks down from above. The open water in the middle of the lake is called the **open-water zone** or **pelagial**. It has no contact with the shore or the bottom. Here live mainly **plankton** and fish.

In summer the sun warms the surface water. This warm water, the **epilimnion**, then lies on the cold deep water, the **hypolimnion**. In between, the temperature changes quickly. In autumn the surface cools down, and the water of the lake mixes again.

gewusst: With its rhizomes, reed can colonise large areas and protects the bank from waves.
Water is heaviest at about 4 degrees. That is why the bottom of deep lakes often has about this temperature all year round.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, certain environmental organisations may lodge an appeal against building projects. This is called the **right of associations to appeal**. In this way nature, which cannot defend itself, gets a voice in court.
wichtigste: The right of associations to appeal was first anchored in the Nature and Cultural Heritage Act (NCHA).
The Environmental Protection Act (EPA) also regulates it, in Art. 55.
The Federal Council determines which organisations have the right to appeal.
The organisation must be active throughout Switzerland and pursue non-profit aims.
Since 2007, organisations that lose bear the costs of the proceedings.
In 2008, voters clearly rejected an initiative to restrict it severely.

abschnitte.text: With many building projects, nobody who stands up for nature and landscape is personally affected. Without an appeal, no court would check whether **environmental law** had been applied correctly. The right of associations to appeal makes this check possible. Supporters see in it an important protection of nature. Critics say it can delay building projects.

The right was first anchored in **Art. 12** of the **Nature and Cultural Heritage Act** (NCHA). Later **Art. 55** of the **Environmental Protection Act** (EPA) was added. It applies to facilities that need an **environmental impact assessment** (EIA). This is a careful check of how much a project burdens the environment.

Not every association may lodge an appeal. The organisation must be active **throughout Switzerland** and pursue purely **non-profit aims**. Since the revision of 2007, the environment must also have been part of its statutory purpose for at least **ten years**. The **Federal Council** names the eligible organisations in an ordinance. These include, for example, Pro Natura, WWF Switzerland and the Foundation for Landscape Protection.

With the revision of 2007, the rules were tightened. If an organisation loses, it bears the **costs of the proceedings** like other parties. A popular initiative then wanted to restrict the right severely. On 30 November 2008, about two thirds of voters and all the cantons rejected it. The right of associations to appeal remained.

gewusst: Local nature conservation clubs may not lodge an association appeal, even if they are very committed to their area.
The initiative of 2008 was not accepted in a single canton.

teile.einleitung: The primeval forest of Derborence in the Valais is among the last true primeval forests in Switzerland. Two rockslides shaped the remote valley and protected the forest from use by people for a long time.
wichtigste: Derborence lies in the municipality of Conthey in the Valais, below the Diablerets.
Rockslides in 1714 and 1749 buried alpine pastures and made access difficult.
This created the Lac de Derborence.
The forest is a fir and spruce primeval forest with mighty silver firs.
Charles Ferdinand Ramuz made Derborence known with a novel of 1934.
The landscape has been listed in the federal inventory BLN since 1977.

abschnitte.text: Derborence lies in the municipal area of **Conthey** in the canton of **Valais**, below the mountain massif of the **Diablerets**. The valley is remote and surrounded by high rock walls. Here grows one of the last **primeval forests** in Switzerland. A primeval forest is a forest that has never been used for forestry.

In **1714 and 1749**, huge masses of rock fell from the Diablerets into the valley. The **rockslides** buried alpine pastures and made the valley hard to reach. The rubble also dammed up the Derbonne stream. This created the **Lac de Derborence**, which is slowly silting up. Because the forest was so remote, it stayed untouched.

In the primeval forest grow mainly **silver firs** and **spruces**. Some silver firs are very large and several centuries old. Old trees die naturally here and stay lying or standing. That means there is a lot of **deadwood**. Fungi, beetles and many other living things live in it. A typical resident is the rare **three-toed woodpecker**, which looks for bark beetle larvae in dying conifers.

True primeval forests are very rare in Central Europe. They show what a forest looks like entirely **without management**: with trees of every age, gaps and a lot of deadwood. Researchers can observe here how a forest renews itself. That is why Derborence is protected. The landscape has been listed since **1977** in the **Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments (BLN)**.

The French-speaking Swiss writer **Charles Ferdinand Ramuz** made the valley famous. In his novel **“Derborence”** of 1934 he tells the story of a herdsman who survives the rockslide and returns from the rocks weeks later. The novel was **made into a film in 1985**.

gewusst: Ramuz is shown on the former Swiss 200-franc note.
The Lac de Derborence is getting smaller and smaller over time, because streams carry gravel and sand into it.

teile.einleitung: The Paris Agreement is a worldwide treaty to protect the climate. Almost all the countries of the world have committed in it to limiting global warming. It was adopted in December 2015 at the climate conference in Paris.
wichtigste: The Paris Agreement was adopted on 12 December 2015.
Its central aim is to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees.
The countries are also to make an effort to limit the warming to 1.5 degrees.
Each country decides for itself how strongly it cuts its greenhouse gases.
Every five years, countries are to review and tighten their climate targets.
The agreement entered into force on 4 November 2016.
Switzerland ratified the agreement in 2017 and wants to release net zero greenhouse gases by 2050.

abschnitte.text: The **Paris Agreement**, often called the Paris climate accord, is a treaty under international law. It was negotiated at the 21st **UN climate conference** in Paris, also called COP21. It builds on the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change of 1992. It followed the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, which contained obligations for only some of the countries.

Global warming is to stay well below 2 degrees compared with the time before industrialisation. If possible it is even to be limited to **1.5 degrees**. In the second half of the century, the world is not to release more greenhouse gases than forests and other stores can take up. In addition, countries are to be better able to adapt to the consequences of climate change.

Unlike earlier treaties, the agreement does not set a fixed number for each country. Every state submits its own climate plan, the **nationally determined contribution**. Every five years it is checked whether the world is on course, and the plans are meant to become more ambitious. Rich countries support poorer countries with money for climate protection and adaptation.

Almost all the states on Earth have joined the agreement. The USA has announced its withdrawal twice, most recently in 2025, after rejoining in 2021. The climate conferences take place every year in changing places. There it is negotiated how the aims of the agreement are to be reached.

Switzerland ratified the agreement in 2017. It wants to halve its greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared with 1990. In June 2023 voters accepted the **Climate and Innovation Act**. It states that Switzerland is to reach **net zero** by 2050.

The agreement is seen as a milestone, because for the first time almost the whole world agreed on a common climate goal. Critics complain that there are no penalties if a country misses its targets. Experts calculate that the climate plans so far are not yet enough to keep to 1.5 degrees. Even so, the agreement has speeded up the expansion of solar and wind energy worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: A treaty between several states
To confirm a treaty officially so that it applies to your own country
Not releasing more greenhouse gases than are removed from the air again
The annual climate conference of the United Nations, from the English Conference of the Parties

gewusst: When it was adopted in Paris, the delegates cheered and hugged each other, and many had tears in their eyes.
The agreement came into force faster than expected, only just under a year after the conference.
The signatures of many states were collected on Earth Day, 22 April 2016, in New York.

teile.einleitung: The **Venus flytrap** is a plant that catches animals. With its leaves it snaps shut in a flash. In this way it gets nutrients that are lacking in the soil.
wichtigste: The Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant.
It catches mainly insects and spiders.
Its trap leaves snap shut in less than a second.
Usually the sensory hairs have to be touched twice.
In the wild it grows only in North Carolina and South Carolina in the USA.
After a catch, the trap stays closed for several days.

abschnitte.text: The Venus flytrap belongs to the **carnivorous plants**. Its trap leaves consist of two halves that look like an open mouth. Along the edge sit long **bristles** like teeth. When the trap is closed, they interlock like a grille. In this way the prey cannot escape.

On the inside of the trap sit fine **sensory hairs**. Usually the trap closes only when these are touched **twice** in quick succession. That way it does not snap shut because of a raindrop. The trap closes in a fraction of a second. This is among the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.

After a catch, the trap stays closed for **several days**. During this time the plant releases digestive juices and dissolves the soft parts of the prey. Then the trap opens again. Only hard remains are left.

In the wild, the Venus flytrap grows only in a small area in **North Carolina** and **South Carolina** in the USA. There it grows in wet bogs that are **poor in nutrients**. The soil contains hardly any nitrogen. The caught animals supply it with this important nutrient. It still needs light, because like other plants it carries out photosynthesis.

gewusst: The Venus flytrap can close its trap only a few times, after which the trap leaf dies and new ones grow.
It does not get its food only from insects: like every green plant, it makes sugar itself with sunlight.

teile.einleitung: Vanilla is a popular spice obtained from the fruits of an orchid. Because growing it takes a lot of manual work, real vanilla is among the most expensive spices in the world.
wichtigste: Vanilla is an orchid and grows as a climbing plant.
It originally comes from Mexico, and the Aztecs already used it.
Today Madagascar produces the most vanilla.
Each flower is open for only about one day.
Outside its homeland, every flower has to be pollinated by hand.
The most important flavour substance is vanillin.

abschnitte.text: Vanilla belongs to the **orchids**. It grows as a **liana** and climbs up trees or support posts with **aerial roots**. On plantations the plants are kept at a reachable height so that the flowers and fruits are easy to get at. Each **vanilla flower** opens on only a single day. If it is not pollinated then, it wilts and forms no fruit.

Vanilla originally comes from **Mexico**. The **Aztecs** already flavoured their cocoa drink with it. Spanish conquerors brought it to Europe in the 16th century. Today it is grown in many tropical countries. The most real vanilla is supplied by the island of **Madagascar** in the Indian Ocean. A cyclone there can make prices rise sharply worldwide.

In the home of vanilla, the flowers are pollinated mainly by certain **bees**. Elsewhere these animals are missing. For a long time, vanilla therefore bore hardly any fruit outside Mexico. In **1841**, the twelve-year-old **Edmond Albius** invented a simple method of pollinating the flowers by hand with a small stick. He was an enslaved boy on the island of **Réunion**. His method is still used today.

The fruit of vanilla is a long, green **capsule** that is called a pod. Fresh, it hardly smells. Only during **fermentation**, treatment with heat and drying over several weeks, is the most important flavour substance, **vanillin**, produced. The pod turns dark brown in the process. The tiny **black dots** in real vanilla ice cream are the seeds from the fruit. Today vanillin is also made artificially, because real vanilla is very expensive.

The island of **Réunion** used to be called **Île Bourbon**. The well-known **Bourbon vanilla** is named after it. Today the name is used for vanilla from the region in the Indian Ocean, including from Madagascar.

gewusst: After saffron, vanilla is regarded as one of the most expensive spices in the world.
A single vanilla pod contains thousands of tiny seeds.

teile.einleitung: How does the water get from the roots to the top of a tall tree, without any pump? The answer is the **transpiration pull**. The evaporation of water at the leaves constantly draws new water upwards.
wichtigste: The transpiration pull arises mainly at the cell walls of the mesophyll in the leaf.
The plant gives off over 90 per cent of the water it takes in again.
Most of it leaves the leaf through the stomata.
Warm, dry, sunny and windy weather increases transpiration.
The cooling from evaporation cools the leaf.
With a potometer you can measure the water uptake of a shoot.

abschnitte.text: Inside a leaf lies the **mesophyll**, a tissue made of many cells with air spaces between them. At the damp **cell walls** of the mesophyll, water evaporates into these air spaces. The water vapour then flows out **through the stomata**. Where water evaporates, new water is drawn up from the pipes. This creates a pull that reaches all the way down to the roots.

Water molecules hold tightly together, which is called **cohesion**. That is why the water in the fine pipes of the wood forms a continuous **column of water**. If a part is drawn away at the top, the rest follows like a chain. In the root, the **water potential** is lower than in the damp soil. That is why water flows from the soil into the root. More than **90 per cent** of the water taken up is given off again by the plant into the air.

Transpiration is strongest in **warm, dry, sunny and windy** weather. Dry air takes up a lot of water vapour. **Wind** removes the damp layer of air that lies directly above the leaf, the so-called **boundary layer**. Then even more water can evaporate. In very dry conditions, the plant closes its stomata to save water.

When water evaporates, **evaporative cooling** occurs, much as with sweating. It **cools the leaf** on hot days. That is why it is especially pleasant in the shade of large trees. In lessons, transpiration can be measured with a **potometer**. A cut shoot is placed in a tube of water, and you can see how fast the water level drops.

gewusst: A large broadleaved tree can evaporate hundreds of litres of water on a hot summer day.
Thanks to the transpiration pull, water also reaches the tops of giant redwoods, which grow to over 100 metres.

teile.einleitung: The bank is the strip of land right by the water, for example by a stream. Here water and land meet, and that is why especially many plants and animals live there.
wichtigste: The stream bank is the edge where stream and land meet.
Willows and alders like to grow on the bank, because they like wet soil.
Stinging nettles also like the damp, nutrient-rich soil.
Kingfisher, grey heron and dipper look for their food here.
The beaver is living again on many streams and rivers in Switzerland.
Rubbish never belongs on the bank, you always take it with you.

abschnitte.text: On the bank the ground is often damp or even wet. Not all trees like that. **Willows** and **alders**, however, feel at home here. You often see them in a row along streams. Their roots hold the earth in place. That way the bank is not so easily washed away in a flood.

Many plants grow on a stream bank. A well-known one is the **stinging nettle**. It likes damp, nutrient-rich soil. Its fine **stinging hairs** burn on the skin when you touch them. For the caterpillars of many butterflies, however, the nettle is an important food plant. In addition there are grasses, sedges and flowers.

The **kingfisher** is blue and orange. It sits still on a branch above the water. If it sees a small fish, it plunges in in a flash. The **grey heron** has long legs and stands calmly in the shallow water. Then it strikes with its pointed beak. The **dipper** can even dive under and look for insect larvae on the bed of the stream.

The **beaver** is a large rodent. With its strong teeth it gnaws down trees on the bank. From branches it builds **dams** and lodges. That way it dams up the water and creates new ponds in which other animals live. In Switzerland the beaver had once disappeared. Today it lives again on many streams and rivers.

A natural bank is a valuable habitat. In Switzerland many streams used to be straightened and lined with walls. Today some are being made **more natural again** so that animals and plants can return. Everyone can help: **rubbish** never belongs on the bank, because it harms animals and pollutes the water.

gewusst: The dipper is the only songbird here that can walk and dive under water.
A kingfisher dives into the water so fast that you can hardly see it.

teile.einleitung: If someone has eaten something poisonous, every minute counts. In Switzerland, **Tox Info Suisse**, the national poisons information centre, helps then. Its emergency number is **145**.
wichtigste: Tox Info Suisse is Switzerland’s poisons emergency line, with the number 145.
The number can be reached around the clock.
If someone is unconscious, call the ambulance number 144 straight away.
Never make someone vomit yourself.
Take a piece of the plant with you so that experts can identify it.
Tox Info Suisse is based in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: **Tox Info Suisse** is based in **Zurich** and can be reached **around the clock**, every day of the year. The calls are answered by **doctors and medical experts**. They say whether a poisoning is dangerous and what to do. Often they can reassure you, because many poisonings are harmless. If necessary, they send the people affected to a doctor or to hospital.

If a poisoned child is **unconscious**, has difficulty breathing or has convulsions, you call **144** straight away, the number for the ambulance. Then an ambulance comes as quickly as possible. The number 145 is for questions and advice, the number 144 for acute emergencies. If in doubt, it is never wrong to get help.

abschnitte.titel: What to do with poisonous plants
abschnitte.text: If a younger brother or sister has eaten a poisonous berry, you first get **an adult**. You should **never make someone vomit yourself**, because that can do more harm than good. When you call, the expert will want to know **what, how much and when** something was eaten. The child’s age and weight are also important. If you go to the doctor, you take **a piece of the plant** with you so that it can be identified.

For **unknown berries** in the forest, there is a simple rule: **never eat them without an adult**. Many poisonous berries look pretty, for example those of deadly nightshade or mezereon. If **plant sap gets into the eye**, you rinse the eye straight away and thoroughly **with water**. Medicines, cleaning products and mushrooms are also among the common reasons for a call. It is best to keep such things out of the reach of children.

gewusst: Many calls to Tox Info Suisse concern small children who have put something in their mouth.
Many calls can be settled with advice over the phone, without a visit to the doctor being necessary.

teile.einleitung: **Peat** is a dark, soft mass that forms in bogs. It consists of plant remains that have not fully decomposed. Peat grows very slowly and preserves traces from past millennia.
wichtigste: Peat consists of incompletely decomposed plant remains.
It forms because oxygen is lacking in the wet bog and the water is acidic.
A layer of peat in a raised bog grows only about 1 millimetre per year.
Light, slightly decomposed peat from the upper layers is called white peat.
In the past dried peat was a fuel, today it is mainly found in potting compost.
Over millions of years, peat can turn into coal.

abschnitte.text: In a **bog** the ground is constantly wet. Dead plants, above all **peat mosses**, sink into the water. There **oxygen is lacking** and the water is **acidic**. Bacteria and fungi, which otherwise break down plant remains, can hardly work as a result. The remains are only **incompletely decomposed** and pile up. That is how peat forms over a long time.

A layer of peat in a **raised bog** grows only about **1 millimetre per year**. So one metre of peat takes about a thousand years. The upper, young layers are light and only slightly decomposed. They are called **white peat**. Further down lies older, more strongly decomposed and darker **black peat**.

Because hardly anything rots in peat, things are preserved for **thousands of years**. Researchers find **pollen** in it, that is, flower dust, as well as wood and sometimes objects from earlier times. **Pollen analysis** examines the pollen from different layers of peat. That way you can tell which trees and plants used to grow in an area. The climate of past times can also be estimated this way.

In the past, peat was cut, dried and used **as a fuel for heating**. Today peat is mainly used for **potting and garden compost**, because it stores water well. Since peat extraction destroys bogs and harms the climate, there is more and more **peat-free compost**. If peat lies under pressure and heat for millions of years, it can turn into **lignite** and later **hard coal**.

gewusst: One metre of peat can contain about a thousand years of plant history.
Bogs store a great deal of carbon, even though they cover only a small part of the land surface.

teile.einleitung: In **vertical farming**, plants do not grow in a field but on floors one above another in buildings. Light, warmth, water and nutrients are controlled exactly. This saves space but needs a lot of energy.
wichtigste: Vertical farming is growing plants on floors lying one above another in buildings.
Many plants use hydroponics, that is, growing without soil in a nutrient solution.
Aquaponics combines fish farming and plant growing in one cycle.
LED lamps give mainly red and blue light.
The biggest disadvantage is the high energy use.
Leafy vegetables and herbs are especially suitable.
The idea became well known around the year 2000 through Dickson Despommier.

abschnitte.text: In a vertical farm, growing areas in halls or high-rise buildings are **stacked**. Light, temperature and nutrients are fully controlled. Because weather and seasons play no part, you can harvest all year round. Together with the many floors, this gives a much higher **yield per area of ground** than in a field.

Many vertical farms work with **hydroponics**. The roots stand in a **nutrient solution**, which supplies all the nutrients in a cycle. Evaporated water is caught and reused. That is why vertical farming often needs much less water than growing outdoors. In **aquaponics**, fish are added too: bacteria turn their waste into nutrients for the plants, and the plants clean the water.

Instead of sunlight, the plants use **LED lamps**. They give mainly **red and blue light**. The green leaf pigment chlorophyll absorbs these colours especially well, while green light is reflected more. That is why many plants glow violet-pink.

**Leafy vegetables** such as lettuce and **herbs** are especially suitable. They grow quickly, stay small and are eaten almost entirely. Staple foods such as cereals would be far too expensive indoors. In a field, cereals need a lot of space but hardly any electricity.

The biggest disadvantage is the high **energy use** for light and air conditioning. This makes the products expensive. Whether the climate balance is good depends strongly on the source of the electricity. The idea was made known around the year 2000 by **Dickson Despommier**, a professor at Columbia University in New York. With students he developed the concept of farms in skyscrapers.

gewusst: In a vertical farm, weather and seasons play no part, so you can harvest all year round.
Many vertical farms glow violet because green light is missing.

teile.einleitung: A tornado is a rapidly rotating column of air that reaches from a thunderstorm cloud down to the ground. It is one of the most violent weather phenomena on Earth. Inside it, the winds can blow faster than in any other storm.
wichtigste: A tornado is a rapidly rotating column of air.
It reaches from a thunderstorm cloud to the ground.
The strongest tornadoes reach wind speeds of over 400 kilometres per hour.
Most tornadoes occur in the USA, especially in the so-called Tornado Alley.
A tornado over a lake or the sea is called a waterspout.
The strength is given on the Fujita scale.
Weak tornadoes also occur occasionally in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: A **tornado** is a rotating column of air that is connected to a thunderstorm cloud and touches the ground. You often see a grey **funnel** or trunk hanging down from the cloud. It becomes visible through water droplets, dust and debris. A tornado is usually only a few dozen to a few hundred metres wide.

Tornadoes usually form in very strong thunderstorms, often in so-called **supercells**. In these, warm, damp air near the ground meets cooler, drier air higher up. If the wind direction changes strongly with height, the air in the thunderstorm begins to rotate. This rotation can extend downwards and turn into a tornado.

The strength of a tornado is measured by the damage it does, using the **Fujita scale**, today in the USA with the extended version EF0 to EF5. A weak tornado blows tiles off roofs, a very strong one can destroy houses completely. Most tornadoes last only a few minutes. Some strong tornadoes, however, travel for over an hour and for dozens of kilometres.

Tornadoes are most common in the United States, where over a thousand are counted per year. Especially affected is **Tornado Alley** in the Great Plains, for example in Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas. There, damp air from the Gulf of Mexico meets dry air from the Rocky Mountains. In Europe, too, there are hundreds of tornadoes every year, but most are weak.

In Switzerland tornadoes are rare, but they do occur. They are mostly weak whirlwinds that last only a short time. Over lakes such as Lake Geneva or Lake Maggiore, **waterspouts** are occasionally seen. But not every storm damage comes from a tornado, and often strong downdrafts from thunderstorms are the cause.

Weather services watch thunderstorms with **radar** and can therefore warn of rotating storm cells. In the USA, sirens wail when there is a danger of tornadoes, and many houses have a storm shelter. If you are caught by a tornado, it is best to find a cellar or a windowless room in the middle of the house. A car, on the other hand, offers hardly any protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very strong, long-lived thunderstorm with a rotating updraft
A tornado over a body of water
A scale used to classify the strength of a tornado by the damage it causes
A trunk-shaped cloud that hangs down from a thunderstorm

gewusst: A tornado can whirl cars and even houses through the air.
In the USA there are researchers who follow tornadoes with special vehicles, and they are called storm chasers.
Tornadoes in the northern hemisphere mostly rotate anticlockwise.

teile.einleitung: The **giant water lily Victoria** has the largest floating leaves of all water plants. Its scientific name is Victoria amazonica. It grows in calm waters in the Amazon region.
wichtigste: The giant water lily grows in the Amazon region in South America.
Its round leaves can grow about 3 metres across.
It was named in 1837 after the English Queen Victoria.
The flower opens in the evening, and in the first night it is white.
In the second night it is pink to red.
The underside of the leaf and the stalks are full of spines.
Air chambers keep the leaves above water.

abschnitte.text: The giant water lily grows in calm waters in tropical **South America**, above all in the **Amazon region**. It is warm there all year round. It roots in the muddy bottom. Its leaves and flowers float on the water surface. The name recalls the English **Queen Victoria**: in 1837 the plant was named after her, just when she had become queen.

The round leaves can grow about **3 metres** across. Their edge is bent upwards, so they look like big baking trays. Under the leaf run thick veins. Between them lie **air chambers**. That is why the leaves are light and float. The underside and the stalks are full of sharp **spines**. They protect the plant from fish and other animals.

The leaves are built very sturdily. If the weight is well spread, a large leaf can even carry a **small child**. In the past, children were put for fun on a board laid on the leaf. The construction of the leaf veins is also said to have inspired the builders of large glasshouses.

The flower opens **in the evening** at sunset. In the first night it is **white** and has a strong scent. In this way it attracts **beetles**, which bring pollen with them. After pollination the flower turns **pink to red** in the second night. The colour shows that the flower has already been visited.

gewusst: A single leaf of the giant water lily is wider than a bed is long.
In some botanical gardens, including in Switzerland, you can see the giant water lily in warm glasshouses.

teile.einleitung: The trophic state describes how many nutrients a lake contains and how much biomass, mainly algae, it produces. It helps experts to assess the condition of a body of water.
wichtigste: The trophic state shows the nutrient supply and productivity of a body of water.
The levels from poor to rich are: oligotrophic, mesotrophic, eutrophic, hypertrophic.
Brown, acidic bog lakes with many humic substances are called dystrophic.
Important measurements are phosphorus, chlorophyll a and Secchi depth.
In eutrophic lakes, oxygen is often lacking in the deep water in summer.
The Swiss researcher Richard Vollenweider shaped water protection worldwide.

abschnitte.text: Experts divide lakes into **trophic levels**. “Oligo” means little, “meso” middling, “eu” good and “hyper” excessive. An **oligotrophic** lake is poor in nutrients, clear and rich in oxygen, like many mountain lakes. A **eutrophic** lake has many nutrients and many algae. A special form is **dystrophic** bog lakes, whose water is brown and acidic because of humic substances.

Above all, the content of **phosphorus** is important, because in many lakes it limits the growth of algae. The amount of algae is estimated from the concentration of **chlorophyll a**, which is found in all algae. A simple measurement is the **Secchi depth**: a white disc is lowered into the water until it can no longer be seen. The more algae, the cloudier the water and the smaller the Secchi depth.

abschnitte.titel: Lack of oxygen in the depths
abschnitte.text: In summer warm water lies on top and cold water below, and the deep water is called the **hypolimnion**. Dead algae sink down and are broken down there. This uses up oxygen, and hardly any fresh supply comes from above. Without oxygen, **phosphate from the sediment** is also released. This internal fertilising can keep a lake rich in nutrients for a long time.

Around the middle of the 20th century, many Swiss lakes were over-fertilised, for example by sewage and detergents. The Swiss researcher **Richard Vollenweider** showed how the input of phosphorus and the renewal of the water determine the trophic state of a lake. Sewage treatment plants and the ban on phosphate in detergents from 1986 helped a great deal. Some lakes in the canton of Lucerne are still artificially aerated today.

A well-known example is the **Burgundy blood alga**, a cyanobacterium. It sometimes turns nutrient-rich lakes such as Lake Murten reddish. Its name recalls the legend of the blood of the Burgundians after the **Battle of Murten** in 1476.

gewusst: Many Swiss lakes are much cleaner today than 50 years ago.
Too few nutrients are not ideal for fish either: in very clear lakes, some fish species grow more slowly.

teile.einleitung: Turgor is the internal pressure in a plant cell. It arises when the vacuole takes up water and presses the contents of the cell against the cell wall.
wichtigste: Turgor is the pressure of the cell sap against the cell wall.
It arises through osmosis: the vacuole takes up water.
The cell wall pushes back with wall pressure and prevents bursting.
If turgor falls because of lack of water, the plant wilts.
Changes in turgor open stomata and move the leaves of the sensitive plant.
In elongation growth, turgor stretches the cell wall.

abschnitte.text: A plant cell has a large **vacuole** full of cell sap. Salts and sugars are dissolved in it. Because of this, water flows into the vacuole by **osmosis**. It expands and presses the cell contents, the **protoplast**, against the cell wall. This internal pressure is called **turgor**. You can compare it to an inflated balloon in a rigid box.

The elastic **cell wall** pushes back with an equal force. This counter-pressure is called **wall pressure**. As soon as the two are equal, the cell takes up no more water. That is why plant cells do not burst in pure water. Animal cells, such as **red blood cells**, have no cell wall and can burst in pure water.

Herbaceous plants have little **supporting tissue** and no wood. Their stability depends strongly on cells filled to bursting. If water is lacking, the vacuoles lose volume, and turgor falls. Then leaves and stems hang down limply, and the plant **wilts**. If it gets water in time, it straightens up again.

Plants also use turgor for movements. The **stomata** of the leaves are surrounded by two **guard cells**. When these take up potassium ions and with them water, their turgor rises. Because of their unevenly thick walls, they curve apart, and the opening opens. In the **sensitive plant**, cells in the leaf joints quickly lose water after a touch, and the leaflets fold together.

Turgor also plays a role in **elongation growth**. Plant hormones such as **auxin** loosen the cell wall. Turgor then pushes it apart, and the cell becomes bigger. That is how young shoots and roots grow in length.

gewusst: The turgor in plant cells is often higher than the air pressure in a car tyre.
If you put plant cells in strong salt water, they lose water and the protoplast comes away from the wall. This is called plasmolysis.

teile.einleitung: The vacuole is a space in the cell filled with liquid. In plant cells it is especially large and has many jobs: it stores substances, keeps the cell firm and protects against animals that eat the plant.
wichtigste: The vacuole is surrounded by a membrane, the tonoplast.
It is filled with cell sap, mainly water with dissolved substances.
In fully grown plant cells it can take up to about 90 per cent of the volume.
The pressure of the filled vacuole is called turgor and makes leaves firm.
If water is lacking, the vacuoles shrink and the plant wilts.
In the vacuole are stored pigments such as anthocyanins as well as bitter and poisonous substances.

abschnitte.text: The **vacuole** is a little sac in the cell that is filled with **cell sap**. This consists mainly of water in which salts, sugars, pigments and other substances are dissolved. A membrane of its own, the **tonoplast**, surrounds the vacuole. It regulates which substances get in and out.

Young plant cells have many **small vacuoles**. As they grow, they take up water and **fuse** into one large **central vacuole**. In fully grown cells it often fills most of the cell, up to about **90 per cent** of the volume. The remaining cytoplasm and the cell nucleus are then pushed to the edge. Animal cells usually have only small vacuoles.

The filled vacuole presses the cell contents against the cell wall. This internal pressure is called **turgor**. It makes parts of the plant that are not woody, such as leaves and young stems, firm. If a plant gets too little water, the **vacuoles shrink**, and the pressure falls. The leaves lose their tension and hang down limply, and the plant wilts.

Many pigments of flowers, fruits and leaves are dissolved in the cell sap. An example is the **anthocyanins**. They give **red cabbage** its colour. Anthocyanins change their colour depending on the **acidity**: in an acidic environment they become reddish, in a basic one bluish to greenish. That is why red cabbage juice can be used as a simple acid test.

The vacuole also serves as a **store**. Plants keep sugars, salts and waste substances in it. Many plants also store **bitter and poisonous substances** there. Animals that feed on the plant are put off by this. That is how the plant protects itself, even though it cannot run away.

gewusst: Whether red cabbage comes to the plate reddish or bluish depends on whether you add acid such as vinegar or apple when cooking.
The word “vacuole” comes from the Latin “vacuus”, which means “empty”, although it is not empty at all.

teile.einleitung: The UNESCO Entlebuch Biosphere lies in the canton of Lucerne between Bern and Lucerne. It is known for its moorland landscapes and shows how nature protection and the economy can go together.
wichtigste: UNESCO recognised the Entlebuch as a biosphere reserve in 2001.
Beforehand, the population had approved the project in votes.
A large part of the area consists of raised bogs and fens.
The region includes the holiday resort of Sörenberg and the limestone wall of the Schrattenflue.
Biosphere reserves belong to the UNESCO programme “Man and the Biosphere”.
They are divided into core zone, buffer zone and development zone.

abschnitte.text: A **biosphere reserve** is not an area from which people are shut out. People live and work here.
