They are to **preserve nature** and at the same time carry on farming, trade and tourism **sustainably**. Areas like this belong to the UNESCO programme “Man and the Biosphere”. The Entlebuch was recognised in **2001**, after the population had said yes in votes.

A biosphere reserve is divided into **three zones**. In the **core zone**, nature has priority. The **buffer zone** protects the cultural landscape that has grown up, such as alpine pastures and bogs. In the **development zone** lie villages, farms and businesses, and farming is done sustainably here. That way protection fits the needs of the local people.

The Entlebuch is one of the areas of Switzerland **richest in bogs**. A large part of the area consists of **raised bogs and fens**. Bogs form where the ground is constantly wet and dead plants hardly rot. They store a lot of water and carbon. Rare plants such as sundew and many dragonflies live here.

A striking mountain is the **Schrattenflue**. It consists of **limestone**. Rainwater has washed deep grooves and gaps into it, which are called **karren** (limestone pavement). The best-known holiday resort is **Sörenberg** in the municipality of Flühli. From there a railway leads up the **Brienzer Rothorn**, the highest point of the canton of Lucerne.

The region even gave its name to a breed of dog. The **Entlebucher Mountain Dog** is the smallest of the four Swiss mountain dogs. It comes from the Entlebuch and used to help farmers drive cattle. Cheese, wood and other products from the region are also sold under the name of the biosphere.

gewusst: The Entlebuch was the first UNESCO biosphere reserve in Switzerland under the new rules of UNESCO.
From above, the karren fields of the Schrattenflue look like a giant labyrinth of stone.

teile.einleitung: The environmental impact assessment, EIA for short, clarifies whether a large construction project complies with environmental regulations. It takes place before building begins, so that damage can already be avoided during planning.
wichtigste: The EIA is anchored in Article 10a of the Environmental Protection Act (EPA).
The details are regulated by the EIA Ordinance of 1988.
An EIA is needed for installations that can significantly burden the environment.
The developer prepares the environmental impact report (EIR).
The environmental protection agency of the canton or the federal government assesses the report.
For cross-border effects, the Espoo Convention of 1991 applies.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the EIA is anchored in the **Environmental Protection Act**. Article 10a requires an assessment for installations that can **significantly burden** the environment. The details are regulated by the **EIA Ordinance** of 1988. Its annex states which installations need an EIA. These include, for example, national roads, large power stations, landfill sites and large shopping centres.

Anyone who wants to build such a project must prepare an **environmental impact report**, EIR for short. In it the **applicant** sets out how the project affects the environment. Areas such as **air, noise, water, soil and nature** are examined. The report also shows which measures can reduce the burdens.

The report is assessed by the **environmental protection agency**. Depending on the procedure, this is the agency of the canton or the **Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)**. The agency gives an assessment. The decision, however, is made by the responsible **decision-making authority**, which takes this assessment into account. The EIA is not a procedure of its own but part of the **permit procedure**, such as the building permit or plan approval.

The great advantage of the EIA: it takes place **before building**. Environmental problems can be solved more easily and more cheaply in planning than later. This corresponds to the **precautionary principle** of the Environmental Protection Act. Burdens are to be limited early, not only once damage has occurred.

Some projects have effects beyond the national border, for example a large power station on a border river. For this there is the **Espoo Convention** of the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) of 1991. It obliges states to **inform and consult** neighbouring countries. Switzerland is a party to this convention.

gewusst: For projects that require an EIA, certain nationwide environmental organisations can lodge an appeal. This is called the right of associations to appeal.
Espoo is a city in Finland where the convention was signed.

teile.einleitung: Tropical rainforests grow close to the equator, where it is warm and damp all year round. They are the forests richest in species on Earth.
wichtigste: There are tropical rainforests in South America, Africa and South-East Asia.
It is warm there all year round, and it rains a great deal.
The forest has several storeys, and it is dark on the ground.
Typical animals are the sloth, toucan, jaguar and poison dart frogs.
The largest rainforest is the Amazon rainforest in South America.
Rainforests are being cleared, which threatens many animals and plants.

abschnitte.text: Tropical rainforests grow in a belt around the **equator**. There are large rainforests in South America, in Central Africa and in **South-East Asia**. The largest is the **Amazon rainforest**. It is warm there all year round. It rains almost every day, and the air is very damp. There is no winter as we have it.

The rainforest is built like a house with several storeys. At the very top, a few **giant emergent trees** stick out. Below them, the treetops form a dense **canopy**. Further down grow smaller trees and shrubs. On the **forest floor** it is darkest, because the leaves above block almost all the sunlight.

Many animals live high up in the trees. The **sloth** hangs upside down from the branches and moves very slowly. The **spider monkey** holds on with its long tail, as if it had a fifth hand. The **toucan** stands out with its huge, colourful beak. The beak looks heavy, but is very light.

The **jaguar** is the largest big cat in the Americas. It creeps through the rainforest and can even swim well. Very small but dangerous are the **poison dart frogs**. Their bright colours warn enemies: careful, I am poisonous! The poison is in their skin.

Very many different animals and plants live in the rainforest, many of them found nowhere else. Plants such as **cocoa**, vanilla and rubber originally come from rainforest regions. The trees store a lot of carbon and are important for the climate. Unfortunately, large areas are being **cleared**, for example for pastures, fields or timber.

gewusst: In a rainforest, hundreds of different insect species can live on a single large tree.
Because there is so much light at the top and so little below, some plants grow directly on the branches of other trees.

teile.einleitung: A dead tree is not simply rubbish. **Deadwood** is an important habitat in the forest. Many beetles, fungi, birds and other animals need it to live.
wichtigste: Deadwood means dead trees and branches.
Fungi break down deadwood especially strongly.
The stag beetle spends its larval stage in rotting oak wood.
Woodpeckers find plenty of food in rotting wood.
Hedgehogs like to hibernate in heaps of branches and leaves.
Foresters leave some dead trees standing as habitat.

abschnitte.text: **Deadwood** is the name for **dead trees and branches**. There is standing deadwood, that is, dead trees that are still upright. And there is lying deadwood, for example fallen trunks or branches on the ground. The **tree stump** that stays in the ground after felling also counts. Depending on the type of wood and the moisture, it takes many years to decades until deadwood has disappeared completely.

**Fungi** break down deadwood most strongly. Their fine threads grow deep into the wood and make it soft and rotten. After that, beetles, woodlice, worms and bacteria help. In the end, **humus** is produced, fertile soil. The nutrients from the wood in this way benefit the living trees again.

Many beetles lay their eggs in the wood, and their larvae eat their way through it. **Many small bore holes** in a dead trunk often show that **beetles live** there. The **stag beetle**, the largest beetle in Europe, spends its larval stage of several years in **rotting oak wood**. Because there are fewer old oaks and less deadwood, it has become rare.

**Woodpeckers** find many beetle larvae in rotting wood. They also hack holes in dead trees. Later, tits, bats or dormice move in there. On the ground, heaps of branches and leaves provide a good winter home, for example for the **hedgehog**. That is why **foresters** deliberately leave some dead trees standing or lying. In Swiss forests there is meant to be more deadwood again today than in the past, so that biodiversity increases.

gewusst: The tinder fungus is a fungus on dead beeches. In the past it was used to make fire.
A dead tree can be almost as valuable to nature as a living one.

teile.einleitung: Ultraviolet radiation, UV radiation for short, is an invisible part of sunlight. In the mountains it is especially strong, and plants and people alike have to protect themselves from it.
wichtigste: UV radiation is invisible to our eyes.
It increases by about 10 per cent for every 1000 metres of altitude.
Fresh snow reflects a large part of the UV radiation.
Many Alpine plants produce red and purple pigments, the anthocyanins, as protection.
Too much UV can damage genetic material and chlorophyll in the cells.
People protect themselves with sun cream, sunglasses and a hat.

abschnitte.text: Sunlight does not consist only of the colours we see. It also contains **ultraviolet radiation**, which is invisible to our eyes. A distinction is made between **UV-A, UV-B and UV-C**. The atmosphere and especially the **ozone layer** block a large part of it. What arrives on the ground can cause sunburn in people and damage plants.

At great height, more UV radiation arrives on the ground than in the valley. The reason: the **layer of air above is thinner** and filters less. For every **1000 metres of altitude**, UV radiation increases by about **10 per cent**. On a **snowfield** the exposure is especially high. Fresh snow reflects a large part of the rays, so you receive them from above and in addition from below.

Too much UV radiation can damage the **genetic material** and the **chlorophyll** in plant cells. High-mountain plants therefore have special protective substances. Many produce **anthocyanins**, pigments that colour leaves and flowers red, purple or blue. In the outer layers of cells they act like a **sun cream**. That is why the flowers of many mountain flowers are so strongly coloured, which also attracts the few pollinators in the mountains.

The radiation first hits the **epidermis** of the leaf. It contains protective substances and is often covered with a **layer of wax**. In this way it blocks a large part of the UV rays before they reach the inside of the leaf. Some Alpine plants are also densely hairy, which also protects.

People too need protection at altitude. Most important are **sun cream, sunglasses and a hat**. They prevent sunburn and damage to the eyes. On glaciers and snowfields it is best to wear good glacier glasses. How strong the radiation is at any moment is shown by the **UV index**, which is given in the weather forecast, for example.

gewusst: Bees can see UV light. Some flowers have patterns that are visible only in UV light and show the insects the way to the nectar.
Even when the sky is cloudy, a large part of the UV radiation gets through.

teile.einleitung: Many plants can make new plants without any seeds at all. A daughter plant grows from a part of the mother plant. This is called **vegetative propagation**.
wichtigste: In vegetative propagation, new plants arise without fertilisation.
The offspring are clones of the mother plant, and their genetic material is the same.
Strawberries reproduce by runners.
Potatoes are propagated with stem tubers.
Ginger forms a rhizome, an underground shoot.
The kalanchoe forms little plantlets along the edges of its leaves.
Low genetic diversity can be dangerous, as the Irish famine shows.

abschnitte.text: In vegetative propagation, new plants grow from body cells of the mother plant. No flower and no **fertilisation** is needed. That is why the offspring have exactly the same genetic material as the mother plant. Such offspring are called **clones**. This is handy for gardeners, because a good variety is kept exactly as it is.

The garden strawberry forms **runners** above the ground. At their nodes, new daughter plants take root. The potato is a **stem tuber**, that is, a thickened underground stem. New plants sprout from its eyes, the buds. Ginger forms a **rhizome**, a horizontally growing underground shoot. If you divide it, new plants arise.

In the **kalanchoe**, finished little plants with roots arise in the notches of the leaf edge. When they fall off, they keep growing on their own. Gardeners also use **layering**: a shoot is bent into the soil and stays connected to the mother plant until it has roots of its own. Only then is it separated.

With **meristem culture**, you grow very many clones from a little tissue. For this, tiny pieces of the shoot tip are placed on a nutrient medium. The tip is often free of viruses. In this way, healthy, virus-free young plants arise in large numbers.

If all plants are the same, they are also equally prone to disease. In the 19th century, only a few vegetatively propagated potato varieties were grown in Ireland. From 1845, **potato blight** destroyed the harvests almost everywhere. The great **Irish famine** followed.

gewusst: From a single leaf, the kalanchoe can form dozens of new little plants.
Many varieties of fruit and potatoes that we eat have been passed on as clones for a long time.

teile.einleitung: Violets are small flowers that often bloom early in the year. The well-known **sweet violet** has a fine, sweet scent. Even a colour is named after the violet.
wichtigste: The colour violet is named after the violet.
The sweet violet smells strongly and is therefore also called the scented violet.
The sweet violet flowers in March and April.
A violet has five petals.
The pansy is closely related to the violet.
Ants carry the seeds of the violet away.

abschnitte.titel: A flower gives the colour its name
abschnitte.text: The word **violet** comes from the Latin name of the violet, viola. Many violets bloom in this blue-purple. But there are also white and yellow violets. Closely related to the violet is the **pansy**, a popular garden flower. Both belong to the same group of plants.
A violet has **five petals**. The lowest petal is larger than the others. At the back it has a small bulge, the **spur**. Nectar for insects collects in it. The flowers stand singly on thin stalks.

The **sweet violet** flowers in March and in April. It is one of the first scented flowers of the year. That is why it is also called the **scented violet**. It likes to grow at woodland edges, by hedges and in gardens. It especially likes half-shady places.

On the seeds of the violet hangs a small, nutritious **appendage**. Ants like it very much. They carry the seeds into their nest and eat the appendage. They leave the seed lying. In this way the **ants** help to spread the violet.
The fine scent of violets has been popular for a long time. It is used for **perfume** and soap. Sweets are sometimes flavoured with violets too.

gewusst: Because ants carry the seeds away, violets sometimes turn up in entirely new places in the garden.
The pansy is actually a violet too.

teile.einleitung: In the past, peat was extracted from many bogs, in Switzerland too. It was used for heating and later for garden compost. Today we know that **peat extraction** destroys bogs and harms the climate.
wichtigste: Cutting peat out with a spade is called peat cutting.
Fresh peat blocks had to dry in the air for a long time.
In Switzerland, a lot of peat was extracted mainly during the two world wars.
During extraction, stored carbon is released into the air as CO2.
In 2012 the Federal Council approved a plan to reduce peat consumption.
Most peat in Switzerland today comes from abroad.
A bog that has been mined takes centuries to millennia to recover.

abschnitte.text: In **peat cutting**, people cut the peat into blocks with a special **spade**. First the bog was drained with ditches. The freshly cut **peat blocks** were heavy and wet. They had to **dry in the air for a long time**, often the whole summer, before they would burn. Then they were used to heat living rooms and stoves.

Switzerland had hardly any coal. Especially **during the two world wars** fuel was scarce, because hardly any coal came from abroad. That is why a great deal of peat was extracted from many bogs at that time. As a result, a large part of Swiss bogs disappeared. In 1987 the people accepted the **Rothenthurm Initiative**. Since then, bogs of special beauty and national importance have been protected by the Federal Constitution.

Peat contains a lot of **carbon**, which plants once took in from the air. When a bog is drained and mined, the peat comes into contact with the air and decomposes. In the process the carbon is released into the atmosphere as **CO2** and makes climate change worse. In addition, **the plants and animals of the bog lose their habitat**, such as sundew, dragonflies and rare butterflies. A bog that has been mined needs **many centuries to millennia** before a thick layer of peat forms again.

Hardly any peat is extracted in Switzerland today. The peat in potting compost comes **mostly from abroad**, for example from Northern and Eastern Europe. In 2012 the **Federal Council** approved a **plan to reduce peat consumption**. Trade and nurseries are to switch step by step to peat-free compost. Substitutes include compost, wood fibre or bark humus.

gewusst: In Switzerland, since the Rothenthurm Initiative of 1987, part of the bogs have been protected in the Federal Constitution.
Peat blocks used to be piled up in stacks to dry, much like firewood.

teile.einleitung: The greenhouse effect makes sure that the Earth is a warm planet that can be lived on. Certain gases in the air hold back some of the heat, much like the glass of a greenhouse. Since humans have been releasing additional greenhouse gases, this effect has become stronger, and the Earth is warming.
wichtigste: Greenhouse gases such as water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane hold heat back in the atmosphere.
Without the natural greenhouse effect, it would be far too cold on Earth, about minus 18 degrees on average.
Thanks to it, the average temperature is about plus 15 degrees.
Burning coal, oil and natural gas releases additional carbon dioxide into the air.
This greenhouse effect strengthened by humans causes climate change.
Since measurements began, Switzerland has warmed about twice as much as the world average.
Scientists were already studying the greenhouse effect in the 19th century.

abschnitte.text: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the ground and the seas. The warm Earth gives the energy off again as invisible **heat radiation**. **Greenhouse gases** in the air swallow part of this radiation and send some of it back to Earth. That way more heat stays near the Earth’s surface, as if under a blanket.

The greenhouse effect is in itself a good thing and vital for life. Without it, the average temperature of the Earth would be about minus 18 degrees, and everything would be frozen. Thanks to water vapour, carbon dioxide and other gases, it is about plus 15 degrees. The most important natural greenhouse gas is **water vapour**.

Since industrialisation, people have burned large amounts of coal, oil and natural gas. This produces **carbon dioxide**, whose share in the air has risen from about 280 ppm before 1850 to over 420 ppm (as of 2024). Cattle farming, rice fields and landfill sites also release the strong greenhouse gas **methane**. Cutting down forests strengthens the effect further.

The French researcher Joseph Fourier suspected as early as the 1820s that the atmosphere warms the Earth. The Irishman John Tyndall showed in the laboratory around 1859 that carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb heat radiation. The Swede **Svante Arrhenius** calculated in 1896 that more carbon dioxide would warm the Earth. Today the IPCC summarises the knowledge on this in large reports.

Switzerland is warming faster than the world average, because land heats up faster than seas. The **glaciers** in the Alps are melting strongly and have lost a large part of their ice since 1850. Hot summers, drought and heavy rain are becoming more frequent. In winter, rain rather than snow falls more and more often at low altitudes.

To slow climate change, fewer greenhouse gases must be released. This includes renewable energies such as sun, wind and hydropower instead of oil and gas. Everyone can help, for example by cycling and taking the train, eating less meat and saving energy. In the **Paris Agreement**, countries have set common goals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that holds back heat radiation
A gas produced by burning and by breathing out, chemically CO2
Short for parts per million, that is, how many out of one million air particles
A long-term change in the climate, today mainly a warming

gewusst: On Venus there is an extreme greenhouse effect, and it is over 400 degrees hot there.
A real greenhouse warms mainly because the glass does not let the warm air escape, so it works somewhat differently from the atmosphere.
Cows release methane when they digest, and it is a much stronger greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

teile.einleitung: **Peat mosses** are small, soft mosses that can build up whole bogs. They soak up water like a sponge. Over a very long time, peat forms from their dead parts.
wichtigste: Peat mosses belong to the genus Sphagnum.
They grow especially often in bogs.
Peat moss stores more than 30 times its dry weight in water.
It keeps growing at the top, while below it dies and turns into peat.
Peat moss makes the water in the bog acidic.
It can be green, red or brown.

abschnitte.text: Peat mosses make up the genus **Sphagnum**. There are many species worldwide, and several occur in Switzerland. They are coloured **green, red or brown**. Peat mosses have no roots. They **keep growing upwards** while the lower parts die off. Over a very long time, **peat** forms from these dead parts.

The little leaves of peat moss have large, empty cells with small holes. The moss stores water in them. Peat moss can take up **more than 30 times its dry weight** in water. If you step on a carpet of peat moss, it feels **wet and spongy**, and water wells up. In the past, dried peat moss was used **as a wound dressing**, because it soaks up a lot of liquid.

Peat moss takes up mineral substances from the water and gives off acid in return. In this way **peat moss makes the water acidic**. In the acidic, wet bog, only a few other plants can grow. Bacteria and fungi also hardly work there, which is why dead moss does not rot properly. That is how peat moss creates its own habitat: the **raised bog**.

Raised bogs made of peat moss have become **rare** in Switzerland. In the past many were drained or mined for peat. Yet they are **valuable for animals and plants**, for example for sundew, cotton grass and dragonflies. Since the **Rothenthurm Initiative** was accepted in 1987, important bogs have been protected by the Federal Constitution. Well-known bog landscapes are found, for example, at Rothenthurm in the canton of Schwyz and in the Entlebuch.

gewusst: A raised bog is fed only by rainwater, and the peat moss gets all its nutrients from it.
Because peat moss inhibits bacteria, it was collected in large quantities for dressings in the First World War.

teile.einleitung: A trophic level shows at which step of the food chain a living thing stands. The word comes from the Greek “trophe”, which means nourishment.
wichtigste: A trophic level is a feeding step in the food chain.
On the first level stand the producers, mostly green plants.
Plant eaters form the second level, meat eaters the third and higher.
Omnivores such as the fox belong to several levels at the same time.
At the very top stand apex predators, which have hardly any natural enemies.
A lot of energy is lost from level to level.

abschnitte.text: At the start of every food chain stand the **producers**. These are mainly green plants and algae. They make their own food with sunlight through **photosynthesis**. All other living things depend on them directly or indirectly. That is why the producers form the **first trophic level**.

Whoever eats plants stands on the **second level**. These animals are also called primary consumers, for example red deer, roe deer or grasshoppers. Animals that eat plant eaters stand on the **third level**. A wolf that eats a red deer therefore belongs to the third level. In the chain grass, grasshopper, shrew, tawny owl, the tawny owl stands on the fourth.

In nature there are not only simple chains but a whole **food web**. Many animals eat different things. An **omnivore** such as the fox eats berries and mice. That puts it on the second and the third level at the same time. Humans are omnivores too.

Animals on the highest level are called **apex predators**. Examples are the orca, the eagle or the wolf. Adult animals are hardly hunted by others. Even so they are not independent: if there is less prey, they too do worse.

Every living thing needs energy for living, moving and keeping warm. Only a small part of the energy of one level reaches the next. As a rule of thumb it is about **10 per cent**. That is why there are far more plants than plant eaters and only a few large predators. This is often shown as a **pyramid**.

gewusst: Fungi and bacteria that break down dead living things are called decomposers. They bring the nutrients back into the soil.
Because of the loss of energy, food chains are usually only a few steps long.

teile.einleitung: Plants do not sweat as we do, but they constantly give off water into the air. This release of water vapour through the leaves is called transpiration. It makes sure that water gets from the roots up to the highest treetop.
wichtigste: Transpiration is the release of water vapour through the leaves.
The water escapes mainly through tiny stomata on the underside of the leaf.
The evaporation creates a pull that draws water up from the roots.
Most of the water taken up, often over 90 per cent, evaporates again.
Transpiration cools the leaves on hot days.
In drought, plants close their stomata to save water.
Heat, wind, light and dry air increase transpiration.

abschnitte.text: **Transpiration** is the evaporation of water from the above-ground parts of a plant, mainly from the leaves. The water leaves the leaf as invisible water vapour. The main route is through the **stomata**, tiny pores that can open and close. A small part also evaporates directly through the wax layer on the surface of the leaf.

A stoma consists of two bean-shaped **guard cells** that form a gap between them. On a single leaf there are thousands of them, mostly on the underside. Through the openings, carbon dioxide also gets into the leaf, which the plant needs for photosynthesis. So the plant has to weigh up taking in carbon dioxide against saving water.

When water evaporates from the leaf, more water is drawn up from the fine pipes. Because water molecules stick to each other, a continuous thread of water forms all the way to the root. In this way the **transpiration pull** draws the water upwards in the vessels, without any pump. Together with the water, minerals from the soil travel to the leaves.

On hot, sunny and windy days, much more water evaporates than on cool, damp days. A large broadleaved tree can give off several hundred litres of water on a hot summer day. When the water in the soil becomes scarce, the plant closes its stomata, and the leaves begin to **wilt**. Cacti save water by having spines instead of leaves and a thick layer of wax.

Through transpiration, plants cool themselves and their surroundings. That is why it is more pleasant in the shade of a tree or in a park than in a car park. Forests give off so much water vapour that new clouds and rain can form from it. In the Amazon rainforest, a large part of the rain comes from the **evaporation** of the trees themselves.

On a sunny day, put a transparent plastic bag over a leafy twig and tie it shut. After a few hours you can see small drops on the inside. This is water vapour from the leaves that has **condensed** into water on the plastic skin. The experiment shows how much water a plant constantly gives off.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny opening in the leaf through which gases and water vapour flow
Two cells that open and close a stoma
The conducting tissue in which water flows upwards from the root
The change from liquid water to water vapour

gewusst: A maize plant evaporates more than a hundred litres of water during its life.
Without transpiration, tall trees could not carry their water up to the crown.
Many plants open their stomata in the morning and partly close them in the midday heat.

teile.einleitung: The **tractor** is the most important vehicle on the farm. It pulls machines across the field, transports loads and lifts heavy things. In Switzerland you see it on fields, meadows and mountain roads.
wichtigste: On the field, a tractor pulls machines such as a plough, harrow or seed drill.
Most tractors run on diesel.
On many tractors the rear wheels are especially large.
With the front loader you can lift heavy things.
On modern tractors the driver sits in a cab.
In Switzerland, with a category G licence you may drive a small tractor from the age of 14.

abschnitte.text: A tractor has a powerful engine that usually runs on **diesel**. On many tractors the **rear wheels** are especially large. Their coarse treads grip well in soft ground so that the tractor does not spin. On modern tractors the driver sits in a closed **cab**, which protects against weather, noise and dust. At the back the tractor has a **power take-off**, a rotating shaft that drives attached machines.

For arable farming, the tractor pulls a **plough**, which turns the soil over. Then the **harrow** breaks up the coarse clods. With the **seed drill**, the seeds are put into the ground in even rows. To spread manure on the field, the farmer attaches a **manure spreader**. That way a single vehicle can do many different jobs.

At the front, many tractors have a **front loader**. This is a bucket or fork on two arms that can be raised and lowered hydraulically. It is used to load manure, soil or heavy **hay bales**. On trailers, the tractor transports fodder, wood or harvest. In winter, some farmers also use it to clear snow in their municipality.

In Switzerland, with a driving licence of **category G** you may drive a small agricultural tractor from the age of **14**. A test is needed for this. On steep mountain meadows, farmers often use special, low vehicles that do not tip over so easily. In the past there were also Swiss tractor firms, for example **Hürlimann** from Wil in the canton of St Gallen. Before there were tractors, horses and oxen pulled the plough.

gewusst: The first tractors were driven by steam and were huge and heavy.
Modern tractors can be steered by satellite and follow their track across the field to the centimetre.

teile.einleitung: Some plants only flower once they have been through a winter. This promotion of flowering by a longer period of cold is called **vernalisation**. The word comes from the Latin ver for spring.
wichtigste: Vernalisation is the promotion of flowering by a longer period of cold.
Most effective is usually about 0 to 10 °C over several weeks.
Winter wheat is sown in autumn because it needs the winter cold.
Biennial plants such as the sugar beet flower only after the winter.
The cold is sensed mainly in the shoot meristem.
In thale cress, cold switches off the gene FLC.
Every new generation has to experience a winter itself.

abschnitte.text: Many plants need several weeks of cold before they can flower. In this way they make sure they do not flower already in autumn but only in spring. Most effective are usually cool temperatures of about **0 to 10 °C**. Hard frost is not needed for this. The cold is sensed mainly in the shoot tip, in the **shoot meristem**. This is a tissue from which new shoots grow.

**Winter wheat** is sown as early as autumn. It germinates, spends the winter as a small plant and forms ears the following year. If it is sown only in spring, it often stays stuck at the leaf stage. It then forms hardly any ears. Spring cereals, on the other hand, need no cold and are sown in spring.

The **sugar beet** is biennial. In the first year it stores sugar in the beet. After the winter it shoots up and flowers. It is similar with carrots or cabbage. Because we harvest the beets already in the first year, we rarely see their flowers.

In **thale cress**, a small experimental plant, the process is known exactly. The gene **FLC** inhibits flowering. Long cold silences this gene permanently, through changes to the **chromatin**, the packaging of the genetic material. In this way the plant remembers the winter. During seed formation, however, this is reset. Every new generation has to experience a winter itself.

abschnitte.titel: A wrong turn in the Soviet Union
abschnitte.text: In the Soviet Union, **Trofim Lysenko** promoted the cold treatment of seed. He called it **yarovisation**, after the Russian word for spring cereal. Lysenko promised exaggerated harvest successes. He combined the method with false theories of heredity that have been scientifically disproved.

gewusst: The plant “remembers” the winter for weeks, although it has no brain.
The acquired state of cold is not passed on to the seeds.

teile.einleitung: The Big Bang is the beginning of our universe. According to the Big Bang theory, the universe arose about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state. Since then it has been expanding and has produced stars, galaxies and planets.
wichtigste: The universe arose about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state.
The Big Bang was not an explosion in a space, but space itself began to expand.
To this day the universe continues to expand.
The Belgian researcher Georges Lemaître developed the idea in the 1920s.
Edwin Hubble observed in 1929 that distant galaxies are moving away from us.
The cosmic background radiation is regarded as the afterglow of the Big Bang.
In the first minutes, the atomic nuclei of hydrogen and helium formed.

abschnitte.text: The **Big Bang** describes the beginning of space, time and matter. At that time everything was unimaginably hot and squeezed together into a tiny space. Since then the universe has been expanding and cooling down as it does so. What was before the Big Bang, or whether there was a “before” at all, science cannot answer to this day.

In the first minutes, the atomic nuclei of the lightest elements formed, mainly **hydrogen** and helium. For about 380,000 years the universe was a hot, opaque fog. Then it became cool enough for atoms to form, and light could travel freely. After a few hundred million years, the first stars lit up.

abschnitte.titel: How did people come up with it?
abschnitte.text: The Belgian priest and physicist **Georges Lemaître** proposed in 1927 that the universe is expanding. The American **Edwin Hubble** showed in 1929 that galaxies move away faster the further away they are. If you run this movement backwards, everything was once together at one point. The name “Big Bang” comes from the astronomer Fred Hoyle, who in 1949 called the theory that, rather mockingly.

In 1964, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson by chance discovered a faint noise coming from all directions of the sky. It is the **cosmic background radiation**, the cooled-down light from the early days of the universe. The amounts of hydrogen and helium in space also fit the calculations exactly. Space telescopes such as the James Webb Telescope see galaxies whose light has been travelling for over 13 billion years.

abschnitte.titel: From the Big Bang to us
abschnitte.text: Stars and galaxies such as our Milky Way formed from clouds of gas. In stars, heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron were made. About 4.6 billion years ago the Sun and the Earth formed. So the substances we are made of were once produced in stars.

At **CERN** near Geneva, researchers smash tiny particles together with enormous energy. For a moment this creates conditions like those shortly after the Big Bang. In this way they hope to understand what the early universe was made of. Swiss universities also take part in large space missions.

begriffe.erklaerung: Everything that exists, that is, space, time, stars and galaxies together
A huge collection of billions of stars, for example the Milky Way
Faint radiation from all directions, the afterglow of the Big Bang
The distance that light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres

gewusst: A small part of the hiss on old tube televisions came from the cosmic background radiation.
When we observe distant galaxies, we are looking into the past, because their light has been travelling for so long.
The Big Bang was silent, because in empty space there is no air that could carry sound.

teile.einleitung: Environmental DNA, eDNA for short, is genetic material that living things release into their surroundings. From a sample of water or soil, you can find out which species live in a place.
wichtigste: Living things constantly lose cells, mucus, hair or droppings, and with them DNA.
This DNA can be obtained from samples of water, soil or air.
In this way species are detected without seeing or catching them.
With metabarcoding, many species in one sample are identified at the same time.
With quantitative PCR, you search specifically for a single species.
eDNA breaks down quickly in water and mostly shows only the recent presence of a species.

abschnitte.text: Every living thing leaves traces. Fish lose mucus and scales, mammals hair, and all of them excrete droppings. In these is their **DNA**, their genetic material. These traces in the environment are called **environmental DNA** or **eDNA**. Researchers filter water, for example, and examine which DNA is in it.

The great advantage: you **neither have to see nor catch** the animals. A water sample can show that a shy fish or a rare newt lives in the water. The animals are not disturbed in the process. **Non-native species** can also be discovered early in this way. In Switzerland, experts at **Eawag**, the federal water research institute, for example, are researching with this method.

If you want to detect **a single species**, you usually use **quantitative PCR**. In this, species-specific primers copy only the DNA of the species being sought. The measurement shows whether and how much of it is present. In **metabarcoding**, by contrast, you copy a typical stretch of DNA from all the organisms in the sample and read it out. A comparison with a **reference database** shows which species are present. If a species is missing from the database, it goes undetected.

abschnitte.titel: What eDNA reveals and what it does not
abschnitte.text: Free DNA is broken down in water by **UV light, heat and microbes**, often within days to weeks. A detection therefore usually means that the species was there a short time ago. In a river, the DNA is also carried **with the current** downstream. A sample can therefore contain DNA from animals that live further upstream.

Even tiny traces of DNA can be detected. That is why equipment or hands can easily **contaminate** a sample. Researchers wear gloves and take **blank samples** of clean water with them. If a blank sample shows DNA, the measurement is doubtful and has to be repeated.

gewusst: With eDNA from the air, researchers in zoos were able to show which animals live nearby.
A few litres of water from a lake can contain DNA from dozens of fish species.

teile.einleitung: Truffles are fungi whose tuber-like fruiting bodies grow underground. Because of their strong aroma, they are among the most expensive foods in the world.
wichtigste: Truffles grow underground and cannot be seen from outside.
They live in a partnership with tree roots, for example of oak, beech and hazel.
Today truffles are mostly searched for with trained dogs.
The white Alba truffle from Piedmont is regarded as the most expensive.
In Switzerland the Burgundy truffle grows most often.
In the kitchen, truffles are usually shaved raw into thin slices.

abschnitte.text: Truffles are **fungi**. The part that is eaten is their **fruiting body**. It looks like a small tuber and grows in the ground. That is why you cannot see truffles from outside. Ripe truffles give off a very strong scent. It attracts animals such as **wild boar**, which dig them up and eat them. With their droppings they spread the spores in other places.

Truffles cannot grow alone. They form a **mycorrhiza**, a partnership with the roots of broadleaved trees such as **oaks, beeches and hazel bushes**. The fungus helps the tree to take up water and nutrients. In return it gets sugar from the tree. For **truffle plantations**, young trees are planted whose roots have been inoculated with truffle fungus. It often takes many years until the first harvest.

Because truffles lie hidden in the ground, you need a good nose. Today people mostly work with trained **truffle dogs**. They smell the ripe tubers and show the spot. In the past, **pigs** were also used. But they like to eat the truffles themselves.

The most expensive kind is the **white Alba truffle** from Piedmont in Italy. It can hardly be cultivated and is collected almost only in the wild. For one kilogram, you often pay several thousand francs. Also well known is the **black Périgord truffle**, named after a region in south-west France. It is harvested in winter. In Switzerland the **Burgundy truffle** grows most often, for example in the Jura and the Central Plateau, and it is harvested in autumn.

Truffles have a very strong aroma that is lost with long cooking. That is why they are usually shaved **raw into thin slices** over a finished dish, for example over pasta, risotto or scrambled eggs. A few grams are enough for a plate.

gewusst: The Burgundy truffle and the summer truffle are now mostly regarded as one and the same species.
Because wild boar love truffles, their tracks are sometimes a clue for collectors.

teile.einleitung: When leaves, branches or food scraps slowly break down, this is called **rotting**. Many small animals, fungi and bacteria help with it. In the end, new soil arises from it.
wichtigste: In rotting, leaves slowly break down into soil.
Soil animals such as woodlice, millipedes and worms shred the leaves.
Fungi and bacteria break down the remains further.
The decomposers need moisture.
In the cold, leaves rot only slowly.
Oak leaves rot especially slowly.
Glass does not rot in nature.

abschnitte.text: In autumn many leaves fall to the ground. They do not stay lying there for ever. In **rotting**, they break down into tiny pieces. In the end, new, dark **soil** arises from them. In this way the nutrients from the leaves come back into the ground. The trees can use them again later.

First come **soil animals** such as woodlice, millipedes and earthworms. They eat the soft leaf tissue and shred the leaves. That is why on old leaves you often see only the fine **network of veins**, because the hard veins last longer. After that, **fungi** and **bacteria** break down the remains further.

The small decomposers need **water** to live. In dry leaves, rotting goes only slowly. **Warmth** helps too. In the cold the living things hardly work, so leaves rot very slowly in winter. In the damp, mild spring, on the other hand, it goes faster.

Not everything rots equally fast. **Oak leaves** are hard and contain a lot of **tannins**. That is why it takes a long time for them to break down. A banana skin in the **compost**, on the other hand, soon turns brown and falls apart. A **glass bottle** does not rot at all. Glass is not broken down by bacteria and fungi and stays in nature for a very long time.

gewusst: Without rotting, more and more old leaves would pile up in the forest year after year.
In the compost at home the same thing happens as in the forest, only faster.

teile.einleitung: Plant cells often have a large space filled with liquid: the **central vacuole**. It is surrounded by a membrane of its own, the **tonoplast**. This envelope decides which substances get in and out.
wichtigste: The tonoplast is the membrane of the central vacuole.
It is a simple lipid bilayer.
The liquid in the vacuole is called cell sap.
The V-ATPase pumps protons into the vacuole.
That is why the cell sap is usually more acidic than the cytoplasm.
Aquaporins let water pass easily through the tonoplast.

abschnitte.text: The tonoplast is a **simple lipid bilayer**, that is, a membrane made of two layers of fat molecules. In it are many **proteins** that work as pumps, channels and transporters. It separates the **cell sap** in the vacuole from the **cytoplasm** of the cell. In fully grown plant cells, the vacuole can fill most of the cell.

An important pump is the **V-ATPase**. It uses the energy from ATP and pumps **protons**, that is, positively charged hydrogen particles, into the vacuole. That is why the cell sap is usually **more acidic** than the cytoplasm. This creates a **proton gradient**, a difference in the amount of protons. **Proton antiporters** use this difference: they let one proton out and bring another substance in instead.

In the tonoplast sit **aquaporins**. These are channel proteins that let water through quickly. When the vacuole takes up water, it presses from the inside against the cell wall. This pressure is called **turgor** and keeps leaves and stems firm. When water is lacking, the turgor drops and the plant wilts.

The tonoplast is **selectively permeable**, which means it lets only certain substances through. That is why the vacuole can store substances separately from the cytoplasm, for example **tannins**, sugars, salts or pigments. Some of these substances would harm the cytoplasm. The red and blue pigments of many flowers and of beetroot are also found in the cell sap.

gewusst: The name tonoplast comes from the Greek “tonos” for tension, which fits the cell pressure.
The red colour of beetroot comes from the cell sap in the vacuoles.

teile.einleitung: When it does not rain for a long time and it is hot, plants come under **drought stress**. They get too little water and have to save it. This shows, for example, in brown leaves in the middle of summer.
wichtigste: In drought, many plants first close their stomata.
Then little carbon dioxide gets into the leaf, and the plant hardly grows.
Heat increases drought stress, because more water evaporates.
Loamy soil rich in humus stores water best.
Spruces with shallow roots suffer especially and are often attacked by the spruce bark beetle.
The sessile oak usually survives drought well thanks to its taproot.

abschnitte.text: Plants lose water mainly through the **stomata** in the leaves. In drought they **close** these openings first to save water. But **carbon dioxide** also gets into the leaf through the stomata, and the plant needs it for photosynthesis. If they stay closed, it hardly gets any building material and **hardly grows**. In **heat**, even more water evaporates, so the stress becomes greater.

In extreme drought, the pull in the water pipes of a tree becomes very strong. Then **air bubbles** can form that interrupt the transport of water. Experts call this **embolism**. Parts of the crown then get no more water and die off. In broadleaved trees, strong drought stress can often be recognised by the **leaves turning brown as early as high summer**.

The **spruce** has **shallow roots**. It cannot reach water from deeper layers of soil and therefore suffers especially badly. Weakened spruces are readily attacked by the **spruce bark beetle**, a small bark beetle. Its larvae feed under the bark and can kill the tree. The **sessile oak**, on the other hand, forms a strong **taproot** that reaches deep into the ground. It therefore usually survives drought well.

How much a plant suffers also depends on the **soil**. **Loamy soil rich in humus** stores water like a sponge and releases it slowly. Sandy soil, on the other hand, dries out quickly. With climate change, hot, dry summers are becoming more frequent in Switzerland, for example in 2018. Foresters are therefore planting more tree species that tolerate drought better.

gewusst: In the hot summer of 2018, many beeches in parts of Switzerland turned brown as early as summer.
Some plants in deserts open their stomata only in the cool night to save water.

teile.einleitung: Emergent trees are the tallest trees in the tropical rainforest. They stick out far above the canopy and are often very old.
wichtigste: Emergent trees are very tall, often old trees in the rainforest.
Broad buttress roots give them a hold on the ground.
On their branches grow orchids and other epiphytes.
The Brazil nut tree and the kapok tree are well-known emergent trees.
The harpy eagle builds its nest high up in their crowns.
When an emergent tree falls, young plants get light.

abschnitte.text: In the rainforest, the treetops form a dense **canopy**. But some trees stick out far above it. They are called **emergent trees**. They can grow to 50 metres and more. At the very top they are especially exposed to sun, wind and rain. Many of these trees are hundreds of years old.

The soil in the rainforest is often not deep. That is why many emergent trees have no deep taproots. Instead they support themselves with **buttress roots**. These are broad, flat roots that stand out from the trunk like walls. They give the tall tree a hold, much like buttresses on a wall. Some buttress roots are so large that a person can hide behind them.

On the branches of emergent trees grow many other plants. They are called **epiphytes**. They include many **orchids**, ferns and bromeliads. They do not grow in the ground but on the tree, because up there they get **more light**. They usually do not harm the tree but only use it as a support.

A well-known emergent tree is the **Brazil nut tree** from the Amazon region. It grows to about 50 metres tall. Its nuts grow in hard capsules. Another giant is the **kapok tree**. Its fruits contain soft fibres called **kapok**. In the past it was used to stuff cushions and mattresses.

In the crowns of emergent trees, the **harpy eagle** builds its nest. It is a mighty bird of prey of the rainforest. When an emergent tree falls, a **gap in the canopy** is created. Sunlight falls on the ground, and young trees can now grow quickly. That is how the forest renews itself.

gewusst: The capsules of the Brazil nut tree are so hard that mainly agoutis, a kind of rodent, can open them.
A single emergent tree can be a habitat for hundreds of different animal and plant species.

teile.einleitung: A dry meadow is a poor, sunny meadow on dry ground. It is one of the habitats richest in species in Switzerland, but it has become rare.
wichtigste: Dry meadows grow mainly on sunny, steep south-facing slopes, for example in the Valais or the Jura.
The soil is mostly shallow, poor in nutrients and lets rainwater drain away quickly.
Many plants have small, hairy or leathery leaves that lose little water.
Grasshoppers, butterflies and lizards such as the European green lizard live here.
Since 1900, more than 95 per cent of dry meadows and pastures in Switzerland have disappeared.
The federal inventory “TWW” has protected the most valuable areas since 2010.

abschnitte.text: Dry meadows form where the ground dries out quickly. This is often the case on steep **south-facing slopes** that get a lot of sun. The soil is thin, stony and **poor in nutrients**. Because hardly any fertiliser is used here, fast-growing grasses cannot push out the other plants. That way many rare, small plants find room.

In summer it gets very hot and dry on dry meadows. Many plants protect themselves with **small, hairy or leathery leaves** that lose less water. Others have deep roots. Typical is **wild thyme**, a low subshrub with strongly scented leaves. Sage, orchids and many grasses also grow here.

Dry meadows are a paradise for animals that love warmth. Especially rich in species are the **grasshoppers**, whose chirping can be heard everywhere in summer. In addition there are many butterflies, wild bees and beetles. On warm slopes in the Valais and Ticino lives the bright green **European green lizard**, the largest lizard in Switzerland.

Most dry meadows were created by people. They stay open only if they are mown or grazed by animals. Without use, shrubs come up first and later trees, which is called **scrub encroachment**. Then the plants that love light disappear. That is why dry meadows are usually mown late in the year and without fertiliser.

Since 1900, more than **95 per cent** of the dry meadows and pastures in Switzerland have disappeared. The reasons are mainly fertilising, building and scrub encroachment. The federal government has therefore created the inventory of **dry meadows and pastures of national importance**, TWW for short. It has been in force since 2010. Farmers who look after such areas receive payments for doing so.

gewusst: Very many different plant species can grow on a single dry meadow, often clearly more than on a fertilised meadow.
Wild thyme is related to the culinary thyme from the kitchen.

teile.einleitung: In **anaerobic digestion**, microorganisms break down green waste, slurry or food scraps without oxygen. This produces **biogas**, which consists mainly of methane. What is left is a valuable fertiliser.
wichtigste: Digestion takes place in several steps and begins with hydrolysis.
Then come acidification, acetic acid formation (acetogenesis) and methane formation.
The methane is made by methanogenic archaea.
Mesophilic plants run at about 37 °C, thermophilic ones at about 55 °C.
Methane formers work best at a pH of around 7.
Unlike composting, you also gain energy as biogas.

abschnitte.text: First comes **hydrolysis**: enzymes split large molecules such as proteins, fats and carbohydrates into small building blocks. In **acidification**, organic acids arise from them. In **acetogenesis**, bacteria convert these mainly into **acetic acid**, hydrogen and carbon dioxide. In the last step, **methane formation**, methane is produced.

The methane is made by **methanogenic archaea**. Archaea are tiny single-celled organisms and form a domain of their own among living things, next to bacteria and all the others. They make methane mainly from acetic acid or from hydrogen and carbon dioxide. They are sensitive to acid and work best at an almost **neutral pH** of around 7.

**Mesophilic** plants run at about 37 °C, **thermophilic** ones at about 55 °C. The higher temperature speeds up the breakdown and kills disease germs. In **wet digestion**, the material can be pumped like slurry. In **dry digestion**, it has more dry matter and is stackable or pasty.

If a **digester**, that is the fermentation tank, gets too much easily degradable material, it goes out of balance. The acid-forming bacteria work faster than the methane formers. The acids pile up, the **pH falls**, and methane formation collapses. That is why a plant has to be fed evenly.

In composting, the energy in green waste is lost as heat. In digestion it stays stored in the **methane**. The biogas can supply electricity and heat or serve as fuel. The digestate is spread on the fields as **fertiliser**. In Switzerland there are many such plants on farms and in municipalities.

gewusst: Methane-forming archaea also live in the rumen of cows.
A digester can turn “sour” from too much feed alone and stop making gas.

teile.einleitung: In a vegetation survey, you note down all the plant species on a marked-off area and estimate how much area each covers. This makes it possible to describe and compare plant communities.
wichtigste: In a vegetation survey, you note all the plant species of an area.
For each species the degree of cover is estimated.
The well-known method comes from the Grisons botanist Josias Braun-Blanquet.
His scale runs from r and + through 1 to 5.
In a forest, the tree, shrub, herb and moss layers are estimated separately.
The area should be at least as large as the minimum area.

abschnitte.text: In a **vegetation survey**, you choose a marked-off area, for example in a meadow or in a forest. You mark it out precisely, for example with **string and pegs**. Then you note **all the plant species** that grow in it. Species outside the area are not counted. Only with a clear boundary can different surveys be compared with each other.

The well-known method was developed by **Josias Braun-Blanquet** (1884 to 1980). He came from **Chur** and is regarded as the founder of **phytosociology**. This science studies which plants regularly grow together. Such groups are called **plant communities**. His scale for estimating cover is still used in many countries today.

For each species you estimate the **degree of cover**. It states what share of the area the plants of one species cover when seen from above. The usual scale runs from **r** and **+** through 1 to 5. “r” stands for “rare”: the species occurs with only one or very few individuals. Level **5** means that the species covers **more than three quarters** of the area. That way you can quickly see which species dominate.

In a forest, plants grow at different heights. From top to bottom, a distinction is made between the **tree layer, shrub layer, herb layer** and **moss layer**. For each layer, the cover is estimated separately. The moss layer is the lowest, lying directly on the ground.

abschnitte.titel: How large the area must be
abschnitte.text: The area must not be too small. Otherwise typical species are missing. Experts speak of the **minimum area**: this is the smallest area on which almost all the typical species of a plant community occur. If you enlarge the area beyond this, hardly any new species are added. In a forest this area is much larger than in a meadow.

gewusst: Braun-Blanquet worked for a long time in Montpellier in southern France.
From many vegetation surveys you can see how meadows and forests change over the years.

teile.einleitung: If you want to know which plants and animals live in a place, you cannot count every single one. That is why experts work with samples. A tried and tested method is the **transect**, a line or a strip along which species are recorded.
wichtigste: A transect is a line or a strip along which species are recorded.
Transects are suited to changes along an environmental gradient.
A belt transect is a strip of a set width.
In the line-point method you note the plant touched at fixed intervals.
Butterflies are often counted on fixed routes in suitable weather.
The Swiss Biodiversity Monitoring uses fixed routes in square kilometres.

abschnitte.text: With a **line transect**, you stretch a measuring tape through an area, for example. Then you note which species occur along this line. A **belt transect**, on the other hand, is a **strip of a set width**, for example one metre. That way you record more area. In the **line-point method**, you look at **fixed intervals**, for example every 10 centimetres, to see which plant touches the tape.

Transects are especially suited to showing changes along an **environmental gradient**. A gradient is a gradual transition, for example from wet to dry or from warm to cold. In the **Alps**, transects are often laid from the valley up to the **summit region**. That way you study the **change of species with altitude**. If the survey is repeated after some years, you can see whether plants are moving higher up because of warming.

Animals too are recorded with transects. **Butterflies** are often counted on **fixed routes in suitable weather**, that is, in sun, warmth and little wind. In **distance sampling**, you also measure the distance of each animal sighted from the line. Animals far away are more easily overlooked. With the distances, the **probability of detection** can be estimated and so the real number of animals can be calculated.

The **Swiss Biodiversity Monitoring** has been observing the diversity of species across the whole country since the early 2000s. For this, experts walk fixed routes in **square kilometres** that are spread across the whole of Switzerland. They record, among other things, **butterflies**, **breeding birds** and plants. Because the same routes are always studied using the same method, changes over the years can be compared well.

gewusst: The word transect comes from the Latin “transsecare”, which means to cut through.
Even a school playground or the edge of a forest is suitable for a simple transect with string and a notepad.

teile.einleitung: Not the same plants grow everywhere on Earth. Large areas with a similar plant life are called **vegetation zones**. They are closely linked to the climate.
wichtigste: A vegetation zone is a large area with a similar plant life.
Above all the climate, that is temperature and rainfall, determines the vegetation zones.
The zones run like belts around the Earth, roughly along the lines of latitude.
The tropical rainforest grows at the equator.
Beyond the boreal coniferous forest, towards the poles, comes the treeless tundra.
On mountains, plant life changes in altitudinal belts.
Above the tree line, closed forests no longer grow.

abschnitte.text: The Sun shines most strongly at the equator, and it gets cooler towards the poles. That is why the vegetation zones run like **belts** around the Earth. They largely follow the **climate zones**. But mountains, seas and winds make the borders uneven. On a map, the zones therefore do not look like straight stripes.

At the equator it is hot and very humid all year round. There grows the evergreen **tropical rainforest** with giant trees. A little further away lies the **savanna**. There the rainy season and the dry season alternate, and mainly grasses grow, with single trees such as acacias or baobabs. In the **desert**, often less than 250 millimetres of rain falls in a year, and only specially adapted plants such as cacti survive.

In the temperate latitudes, where Switzerland lies too, **deciduous and mixed forests** grow naturally. Further north follows the **boreal coniferous forest**, a huge belt of spruces, pines and larches. Even further north it becomes too cold for trees. There lies the treeless **tundra** with mosses, lichens, grasses and dwarf shrubs.

On a mountain, too, it gets cooler as you go up. That is why plant life changes step by step, which is called **altitudinal belts**. In the Alps, deciduous forest, coniferous forest, alpine meadows and rock follow one another, for example. The **tree line** is the line above which closed forests no longer grow. In the Swiss Alps it lies, depending on the region, at roughly 1,800 to 2,400 metres.

gewusst: If you climb a few hundred metres in the Alps, you experience a change in plants similar to a long journey towards the north.
The boreal coniferous forest is one of the largest continuous areas of forest on Earth.
